The rationale for an increased risk of coronary artery disease in ulcerative colitis patients is less obvious. In a meta-analysis of eight studies, IBD was associated with a modest increase in the risk of cerebrovascular disease incidence (HR = 1.29; 95% CI, 1.16–1.43). Both Crohn’s disease (HR = 1.32; 95% CI, 1.13–1.56) and ulcerative colitis (HR = 1.18; 95% CI, 1.06–1.31) were associated with increased risk of cerebrovascular disease ( ). The risk was higher in women (HR = 1.49; 95% CI, 1.24–1.79) than in men (HR = 1.22; 95% CI, 1.12–1.32). In a second meta-analysis of six studies, IBD was associated with a modest increase in the risk of coronary artery disease (odds ratio [OR], 1.19; 95% CI, 1.08–1.31), both in patients with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis ( ). This risk increase was seen primarily in women (four studies; OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.18–1.35), with no significant risk increase for men ( ). In a meta-analysis of five studies, there was a modest increased risk of cerebrovascular disease (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.09–1.27), especially among women (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.17–1.41) compared with men (OR, 1.11; 95% CI, 0.98–1.25) ( ). The increase in risk was observed for patients with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. As the overwhelming majority of the evidence points to increased risks for potentially life-threatening vascular disease in persons with IBD, this adds to the burden of the disease. Further, clinicians need to be vigilant with assessing conventional risk factors for vascular disease in persons with IBD so they can be mitigated. VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM The first population-based report on the incidence of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in IBD patients was from the UMIBDED ( ). In Crohn’s disease, the incidence rate of deep venous thromboembolism (DVT) was 31.4 per 10,000 person-years, and the incidence rate of pulmonary embolism (PE) was 10.3 per 10,000 person-years. In ulcerative colitis, the incidence rates were 30.0 per 10,000 person-years for DVT and 19.8 per 10,000 person-years for PE. The IRR was 4.7 (95% CI, 3.5–6.3) for DVT, 2.9 (95% CI, 1.8–4.7) for PE in Crohn’s disease, 2.8 (95% CI, 2.1–3.7) for DVT and 3.6 (95% CI, 2.5–5.2) for PE in ulcerative colitis. There were no sex differences for IRR. The highest rates of DVT and PE were seen among patients over 60 years old. However, the highest IRR for these events was among patients less than 40 years old, meaning that the younger adults with IBD carry an even greater increased risk for DVT and PE than their unaffected counterparts. These data translate to a rate of DVT or PE of 1 per 200 patient-years. In a multicentred Austrian study of 116 IBD patients who had a history of first VTE, 86 incidents were unprovoked ( ). The probability of recurrence five years after discontinuation of anticoagulation therapy was higher among patients with IBD than patients without IBD (33.4%; 95% CI, 21.8–45.0 versus 21.7%; 95% CI, 18.8–24.6; P = 0.01). After adjustment for potential confounders, IBD was found to be an independent risk factor of recurrence (HR = 2.5; 95% CI, 1.4–4.2). In a subsequent study from this Austrian group, the incidence rate of all VTE was 6.3 per 1000 person-years, which was not dissimilar from the rate reported in the earlier UMIBDED study ( ). Patients with VTE did not differ with regards to sex, underlying IBD or disease duration. Most VTEs (77.1%) were unprovoked, most (77.7%) occurred in outpatients, and most (60.9%) occurred in patients with active disease. In a four-centre Canadian retrospective study, patients admitted under surgeons were more likely than those admitted under gastroenterologists to receive VTE prophylaxis (84% versus 74%, P = 0.016) ( ). Of note, the rate of VTE was the same for those who did and did not receive VTE prophylaxis (2.2 per 1000 hospital days) ( ). Among the 14 VTE events, 79% had received prophylaxis, but only 36% were within 24 hours of admission ( ). The increased risk of VTE is known for hospitalized patients, and most centres currently institute VTE prophylaxis for hospitalized patients with IBD. Because many VTEs occur in ambulatory IBD patients, there is a need for guidance in instituting VTE prophylaxis when IBD patients have acutely or chronically active disease. OSTEOPOROSIS AND OSTEOPOROSIS-RELATED FRACTURE IN IBD Osteoporosis increases the risk of fractures that are associated with significant morbidity, particularly those of the proximal femur (hip), vertebra and wrist and even mortality (related to hip fractures) ( ). A study using the UMIBDED reported that persons with IBD have a 40% higher risk of fracture than do age- and sex-matched controls without IBD (estimated at 40.8 per 10,000 person-years for IBD patients under 40

Because many VTEs occur in ambulatory IBD patients, there is a need for guidance in instituting VTE prophylaxis when IBD patients have acutely or chronically active disease. OSTEOPOROSIS AND OSTEOPOROSIS-RELATED FRACTURE IN IBD Osteoporosis increases the risk of fractures that are associated with significant morbidity, particularly those of the proximal femur (hip), vertebra and wrist and even mortality (related to hip fractures) ( ). A study using the UMIBDED reported that persons with IBD have a 40% higher risk of fracture than do age- and sex-matched controls without IBD (estimated at 40.8 per 10,000 person-years for IBD patients under 40 and 107 per 10,000 person-years for IBD patients aged 40 to 59) ( ). This translates to a risk of fracture at about one per 100 patient-years. The proportion of seniors with IBD is also expected to rise over the next decade. This is consistent with general trends in the population and the compounding prevalence effect (see section 3), which will increase further the rates of osteoporosis-related fractures among IBD patients ( , ). Failure to attain peak bone mass when young and accelerated bone loss in adulthood are associated with an increased risk of fracture later in life ( ). Therefore, it is possible that young persons with IBD with a high burden of inflammation or significant exposure to corticosteroids may suffer from bone mineral loss that would leave them at increased risk of fracture as they age ( ). More aggressive treatment of inflammation earlier in the disease course and the more widespread use of steroid-sparing medication have the potential to decrease the risk of bone disease in IBD ( , ). However, corticosteroids are not the only risk factor for osteoporosis—and more importantly, fractures—in persons with IBD. Hence, anyone with IBD with chronically active inflammatory disease should have their bone mineral density tested ( ). CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE INFECTION In Alberta, the risk of Clostridium difficile infection within five years of diagnosis with ulcerative colitis was 3.4% (95% CI, 2.5–4.6%) ( ). The risk of colectomy was higher among ulcerative colitis patients diagnosed with C. difficile (sub-hazard ratio [sHR] = 2.36; 95% CI, 1.47–3.80). Clostridium difficile increased the risk of postoperative complications (OR = 4.84; 95% CI, 1.28–18.35) and was associated with mortality (sHR = 2.56 times; 95% CI, 1.28–5.10). In a study comparing laboratory diagnoses of C. difficile to administrative database diagnoses of C. difficile , there was a lack of specificity of the administrative diagnoses. Linking the Manitoba provincial database of C. difficile infections with the UMIBDED, investigators reported that individuals with IBD have a nearly fivefold increase in risk of C. difficile infections compared with individuals without IBD ( ). There was no difference found between persons with ulcerative colitis and persons with Crohn’s disease. Among individuals with IBD, exposure to corticosteroids, infliximab or adalimumab, metronidazole, hospitalizations, higher ambulatory care visits, shorter duration of IBD, and higher comorbidities were associated with an increased risk of C. difficile infections. Although C. difficile infections increased mortality among individuals with and without IBD, there was a one-third lower mortality after C. difficile infections among individuals with IBD compared with those without IBD. This study did not report an increase in C. difficile infections over time. In a study from the University of Pittsburgh, it was shown that during the year of a C. difficile infection, having a C. difficile infection was significantly associated with more corticosteroid and antibiotic exposure and increased disease activity, worse quality of life and increased health care utilization (all P < 0.01) ( ). During the next year after a C. difficile infection, patients continued to have increased exposure to C. difficile infection-targeted antibiotics ( P < 0.001) and other antibiotics ( P = 0.02). They also continued to have more clinic visits ( P = 0.02), telephone encounters ( P = 0.001) and increased health care financial charges ( P = 0.001). In a multicentre retrospective cohort study of patients with IBD admitted from 2011 to 2013 to tertiary centres in Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa, and Vancouver, IBD patients admitted to surgeons were less likely to be tested for C. difficile (41% versus 88%, P < 0.0001) ( ). In a 2011 study assessing the Nationwide Inpatient Sample in the United States to identify patients more than 18 years of age with a discharge diagnosis of either Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, 4% had C. difficile infections ( ). Venous thromboembolism was present in 6% of the group with C. difficile infections versus 3% in the group without C. difficile infections ( P < 0.001). After a multivariate analysis after propensity-score matching was performed, C. difficile infection was significantly associated with VTE (adjusted OR, 1.7; 95% CI, 1.4–2.2; P < 0.001). The increased risk was similar for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis with concurrent

the Nationwide Inpatient Sample in the United States to identify patients more than 18 years of age with a discharge diagnosis of either Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, 4% had C. difficile infections ( ). Venous thromboembolism was present in 6% of the group with C. difficile infections versus 3% in the group without C. difficile infections ( P < 0.001). After a multivariate analysis after propensity-score matching was performed, C. difficile infection was significantly associated with VTE (adjusted OR, 1.7; 95% CI, 1.4–2.2; P < 0.001). The increased risk was similar for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis with concurrent C. difficile infection ( ). Even though the rates of C. difficile infection are not increasing, it remains an important infection to recognize. Clinicians need to be vigilant to assess for C. difficile infections in persons with IBD with a flare of diarrhea. It is not yet clear whether immunomodulatory therapy should be interrupted when C. difficile infection is diagnosed; currently, most clinicians maintain immunomodulatory therapy during C. difficile infections (personal observation). MENTAL HEALTH Depression and anxiety disorders are at least twice as common in persons with IBD as the general population ( ). These disorders can antedate the onset of IBD by years ( , ). Hence, the relationship between depression and anxiety disorders and IBD is not just a secondary response to having a chronic disease. However, Ontario women with IBD who became pregnant were more likely to experience mood-related disorders in the post-partum period compared with women without IBD ( ). Notably, women with Crohn’s disease were almost three times more likely to visit physicians for substance-related disorders in the post-partum period compared with women without IBD. The biological underpinning of the relationship between psychiatric disorders and IBD is unknown and not well studied. Fatigue is one of the most common, but poorly understood, IBD symptoms and may also, in part, reflect brain abnormalities ( ). Fatigue is also a manifestation of depression. Fatigue has impacts on employment, social functioning and quality of life. In a population-based longitudinal cohort study in Manitoba with approximately 600 persons answering surveys every three months for one year, a high perception of stress was associated with a flare of symptomatic IBD ( ). In a subsequent study by this group, 485 persons with IBD, answering surveys every three months for one year and submitting stool samples for fecal calprotectin, reported that a high perception of stress was associated with a flare of symptoms. However, there was only a modest association between symptoms and ulcerative colitis, and no association between symptoms and Crohn’s disease ( ). Treatment of depression, anxiety and the management of stress are important for enhancing positive outcomes, reducing nonadherence to medications and increasing quality of life. CANCER Because colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the general population ( ) and because the colon is the predominant site of involvement of IBD, CRC has always garnered special attention in IBD. Pooled results from population-based studies suggest an attenuation in the magnitude of CRC risk in persons with IBD over time ( ). Similarly, Soderlund et al. report a several-fold decrease in CRC mortality over time among three successive cohorts of individuals with IBD in Sweden from the 1960s through 2004 ( ). Population-based data from Manitoba demonstrate a twofold increase in CRC incidence (HR = 1.95; 95% CI, 1.65–2.30) and CRC-related mortality (HR = 2.15; 95% CI, 1.60–2.89) among individuals with IBD as compared with those without IBD between 1987 and 2012 ( ). In a stratified analysis, there was no decrease in HR for CRC mortality in later time periods. Similarly, a recent study from Northern California reported stable CRC incidence rates among individuals with IBD, with a 1.6-fold higher incidence than in the general population ( ). This group also reported a standardized mortality ratio (SMR) for CRC in Crohn’s disease patients of 2.3 (95% CI, 1.6–3.0) and for CRC in ulcerative colitis patients of 2.0 (95% CI, 1.3–2.7) among individuals diagnosed with IBD between 1998 and 2008. However, a recent study from Denmark reported that IBD patients no longer have a higher incidence of CRC ( ), although substantially higher rates of colectomy in IBD patients in Denmark as compared with other jurisdictions may have influenced their findings ( ). A meta-analysis of eight population-based studies reports no overall increased risk of extra-intestinal cancers among individuals with IBD ( ). However, these data were from an era of infrequent use of immunomodulators and biological agents, which have more recently been reported to increase the risks of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (azathioprine/6MP) and both nonmelanoma (thiopurines and anti-TNF) and melanoma (anti-TNF) skin cancers among individuals with IBD ( , ). There is a male predilection for lymphoma at all ages and especially in

rates of colectomy in IBD patients in Denmark as compared with other jurisdictions may have influenced their findings ( ). A meta-analysis of eight population-based studies reports no overall increased risk of extra-intestinal cancers among individuals with IBD ( ). However, these data were from an era of infrequent use of immunomodulators and biological agents, which have more recently been reported to increase the risks of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (azathioprine/6MP) and both nonmelanoma (thiopurines and anti-TNF) and melanoma (anti-TNF) skin cancers among individuals with IBD ( , ). There is a male predilection for lymphoma at all ages and especially in relation to lymphoma diagnosed in the setting of immunomodulatory and biological therapy. While the highest incidence rate for lymphoma in IBD is among older males, just as in the general population, the highest IRR is among younger male adults. A more recent study based on Danish health care databases reports a standardized incidence ratio (SIR) of 1.3 (95% CI, 1.2–1.4) for Crohn’s disease and 1.1 (95% CI, 1.0–1.1) for ulcerative colitis with respect to extra-intestinal cancers ( ). CRITICAL ILLNESS A study using the UMIBDED reported that the risk for intensive care unit (ICU) admission is higher for patients with IBD than population controls (HR = 1.79; 95% CI, 1.58–2.02) ( ). The risk of ICU admission was higher for patients with Crohn’s disease (HR = 2.31; 95% CI, 1.95–2.75) than ulcerative colitis patients (HR = 1.37; 95% CI, 1.13–1.65). From 2000 through 2010, age- and sex-standardized annual incidence rates for ICU admission in the prevalent IBD cohort ranged from 0.55% to 1.12%. Compared with controls admitted to ICUs one year after ICU admission, mortality was 32% higher among patients with IBD. The investigators in that study assessed predictors of ICU admission and health care utilization (HCU) post-ICU admission ( ). Risk factors for ICU admission from the year before admission included cumulative corticosteroid use (IRR, 1.006 per 100 mg of prednisone; 95% CI, 1.004–1.008) and IBD-related surgery (IRR, 2.79; 95% CI, 1.99–3.92). Neither use of immunomodulatory therapies within one year nor surgery for IBD beyond one year prior were associated with ICU admission. In those who used corticosteroids and immunomodulatory medications in the year before ICU admission, the use of immunomodulatory medications conferred a 30% risk reduction in ICU admission (IRR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.50–0.97). Persons with IBD who survived ICU admission had higher health services utilization in the year after ICU discharge than controls. Hence, it was concluded that corticosteroid use and surgery within the year are associated with ICU admission in IBD, whereas immunomodulatory therapy is not. CONCLUSION The burden of extra-intestinal disease is high in patients with IBD. Extra-intestinal disease may arise in any organ system of the body. The most common and complicated extra-intestinal manifestations are other chronic IMIDs. Some IMIDs occur when IBD is active; examples include erythema nodosum and peripheral joint arthritis. Alternatively, other IMIDs like ankylosing spondylitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis run a course that is independent of bowel disease activity (i.e., they may progress even in patients whose IBD is in remission). Recent studies have expanded the scope of IMIDs with associations being made between IBD and IMIDs such as asthma and multiple sclerosis. Moreover, patients with IBD are at higher risk of complications in other organ systems such as osteoporosis, venous thromboembolism and cardiovascular disease. In addition, patients with IBD have a higher risk of cancer, including colon cancer likely caused by their bowel inflammation. Other cancer risks include cholangiocarcinoma in the setting of primary sclerosing cholangitis and lymphoma in the setting of ongoing immunusuppressive treatment. Consequently, patients and care providers need to be vigilant in the surveillance of extra-intestinal manifestations and complications of IBD. Ultimately, the most effective means of preventing or reducing the burden of most extra-intestinal diseases is to treat the underlying inflammation of IBD.

documents.title: ASH 2022 guidelines management multiple myeloma elderly

chunks.content: Introduction Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal malignancy of plasma cells that predominantly affects older adults, with approximately 70% of diagnoses occurring in individuals aged 65 years or older [ , ]. This demographic profile necessitates the incorporation of geriatric assessments into clinical decision-making, with the goal of tailoring treatment intensity according to patient frailty [ ]. The International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) frailty score has emerged as the benchmark model for frailty classification in MM, combining the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living (ADL), and the Lawton Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) scale to stratify patients as fit, intermediate-fit, or frail [ ]. Evidence indicates that patients categorized as frail are at increased risk of early mortality, treatment-related toxicity, and therapy discontinuation [ ]. Although comorbidity profiling remains an essential component of risk assessment for frailty, the conventional CCI-based approach has several methodological limitations that compromise its clinical utility and predictive accuracy. First, the comorbidity component relies on the conventional CCI, which assigns fixed weights to 19 conditions without accounting for disease-specific relevance or covariate interactions (Table ) [ ]. This approach may limit its predictive performance in modern statistical modeling [ , ]. Second, the IMWG model reduces CCI to a binary indicator (one point for CCI ≥ 2; see Table ), potentially losing clinically meaningful gradations of comorbidity burden and overlooking clinically relevant disease burden such as renal impairment. In addition, while the IMWG frailty score aimed to improve risk stratification by incorporating functional measures such as ADL and IADL, it presents several limitations in clinical practice. These measures are susceptible to transient impairment from acute disease-related symptoms at the time of diagnosis, reflecting acute disease burden rather than baseline functional capacity. As a result, frailty assessments based on functional status at diagnosis may overestimate patient vulnerability, potentially leading to undertreatment of patients who could tolerate intensive therapy after disease control. Furthermore, the IMWG score applies equal weight to comorbidity (CCI ≥ 2), functional decline (ADL/IADL), and age, without empirical validation of potential interactions or relative prognostic importance of each domain. This fixed-point structure may inadequately represent the clinical complexity of real-world patients, particularly those whose physical limitations are reversible after initiation of therapy [ , ]. These limitations underscore the need for a more adaptable and disease-specific comorbidity-based prognostic model for MM. Given these limitations and the availability of large-scale real-world datasets, we developed a refined comorbidity-based prognostic model specifically for MM patients. Our objectives were to construct a statistically robust risk score using nationwide data, demonstrate its independent prognostic value when adjusted for established staging systems, including the Second Revision of the International Staging System (R2-ISS) [ ] and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, and validate its clinical applicability across different frontline treatment intensities. Materials and methods Study design and data source This retrospective cohort study was divided into two parts: (I) development of the scoring system and (II) its validation. In Part I, a comorbidity-based scoring model, referred to as the multiple myeloma-specific comorbidity index (MM-CI), was developed using national claims data from the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) database, which provides comprehensive healthcare utilization data for the entire population of South Korea. The HIRA database covers approximately 50 million Koreans and includes demographic variables such as age and sex, along with healthcare data encompassing all medical claims and mortality information [ ]. In Part II, to address concerns regarding the reliability and quality of claims-based data sources [ ], we externally validated the MM-CI model using multicenter registry data from both Korean and Japanese populations. For the Korean population, validation was conducted using data from the CARE-MM registry—which includes both prospectively and retrospectively collected clinical information from five university hospitals—as well as data from the Seoul National University (SNU) registry [ – ]. For the Japanese population, we utilized real-world registry data from The Jikei University School of Medicine. In addition, to examine whether the MM-CI maintained prognostic utility across clinically relevant subgroups, we performed subgroup analyses in patients with available data on R2-ISS stage, ECOG performance status, and frontline treatment intensity. The study utilizing HIRA data was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Seoul St. Mary’s Hospital, Seoul, Korea (No. KC21ZNSI0448). As this analysis involved publicly available, anonymized, and de-identified data, the requirement for informed consent was waived. Validation studies using data from Seoul National University Hospital and The Jikei University School of Medicine were approved by their respective institutional review boards (IRB Nos. H-2101-119-1190 and 37-003(12639), respectively). For all study components, informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the data. This research was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Study population MM patients were identified using the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth

the Institutional Review Board of Seoul St. Mary’s Hospital, Seoul, Korea (No. KC21ZNSI0448). As this analysis involved publicly available, anonymized, and de-identified data, the requirement for informed consent was waived. Validation studies using data from Seoul National University Hospital and The Jikei University School of Medicine were approved by their respective institutional review boards (IRB Nos. H-2101-119-1190 and 37-003(12639), respectively). For all study components, informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the data. This research was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Study population MM patients were identified using the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10 code C90), from medical claims data in the HIRA database between January 2007 and November 2022. Patients with a primary or secondary diagnosis of MM (C90) were identified, resulting in a raw cohort of 31,769 patients. Sequential exclusion criteria were applied to refine the final development cohort: (i) patients with a single diagnosis code for MM (C90) ( n = 4406), (ii) patients diagnosed before the age of 19 years ( n = 12), (iii) those diagnosed in 2007 or 2008 to ensure a minimum of one year for comorbidity profiling ( n = 3767), (iv) patients without the cancer-specific co-payment code (V193) ( n = 2160), (v) patients who died within six months without receiving MM-targeted treatment ( n = 1209), (vi) patients who did not receive MM-specific medication ( n = 2900), and (vii) patients with an uncertain index date ( n = 42). This resulted in a final development cohort of 17,273 MM patients (Fig. ). The index date was defined as the start date of first MM-targeted therapy. Specific definitions of MM-targeted therapy codes for frontline therapy, including melphalan, bortezomib, thalidomide, or lenalidomide, based on the HIRA public health insurance criteria, are provided in Table [ ]. For external validation in Part II of the study, two independent real-world datasets were used: (1) a Korean multicenter registry cohort comprising patients from the CARE-MM and SNU registries, and (2) a Japanese cohort consisting of patients treated at Jikei University Hospital. The same eligibility criteria were applied to both cohorts. Patients were included if they (i) had a confirmed diagnosis of multiple myeloma, (ii) were aged ≥19 years at diagnosis, and (iii) had received MM-directed frontline therapy. Exclusion criteria included (i) a diagnosis of plasma cell leukemia, solitary plasmacytoma, or AL amyloidosis; (ii) no initiation of MM-specific treatment; (iii) missing comorbidity data; or (iv) insufficient follow-up to assess survival outcomes (<6 months). A total of 1473 patients were included from the Korean registries and 314 patients from the Japanese cohort (Validation cohort I and II, respectively, Fig. ). Given the distinct treatment landscapes and healthcare systems in the two countries, the validation analyses were conducted independently within each cohort. Definitions For the development cohort, baseline characteristics were collected at the index date, defined as the start date of frontline MM-targeted therapy. Comorbidity profiles were identified using ICD-10 diagnostic codes classified according to the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) recorded before the index date (Table ) [ ]. These codes were selected based on established mappings and were refined through clinical expert review to align with the structure and terminology of Korea’s national claims system [ – ]. Due to limitations inherent in claims data, several diagnostic categories were modified. The severity of liver disease and the presence of end-organ damage from diabetes could not be reliably distinguished; therefore, mild and moderate-to-severe liver disease were combined into a single composite variable, labeled “hepatic disease”. Diabetes was treated as a binary variable, without differentiating for end-organ damage. Additionally, diagnoses of leukemia, lymphoma, and solid tumors were consolidated into a unified “cancer” category. Comorbidities were considered present if listed as a primary diagnosis or if recorded as at least two separate secondary diagnoses within one year prior to the index date. For validation cohorts, R2-ISS scoring was calculated using component weights as previously described [ ]: ISS-II (1 point), ISS-III (1.5 points), del(17p) (1 point), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1 point), t(4;14) (1 point), and 1q gain/amplification (0.5 points). Frontline treatment intensity was defined by the number of major drugs used in frontline treatment, categorized as doublet, triplet, or quadruplet regimens for the validation analyses (Table ). Statistical analysis Continuous variables were summarized using median with interquartile range (IQR). Categorical variables were presented using frequencies and percentages. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were employed to evaluate candidate predictors and construct a scoring model. Complete case analysis was conducted, as the proportion of missing data was less than 5% across all datasets. For the scoring system development in Part I, candidate predictors with a p -value < 0.05 in the univariable analysis were included in the multivariable model to identify factors associated with overall survival (OS). Multicollinearity was assessed using

for the validation analyses (Table ). Statistical analysis Continuous variables were summarized using median with interquartile range (IQR). Categorical variables were presented using frequencies and percentages. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were employed to evaluate candidate predictors and construct a scoring model. Complete case analysis was conducted, as the proportion of missing data was less than 5% across all datasets. For the scoring system development in Part I, candidate predictors with a p -value < 0.05 in the univariable analysis were included in the multivariable model to identify factors associated with overall survival (OS). Multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors, and multivariable analysis was conducted using the Cox proportional hazard regression model after confirming the proportional hazards assumption using Schoenfeld residuals. Stepwise selection was employed to establish the scoring system from candidate predictors, with the Akaike information criterion as the metric for comparison. In addition, to balance statistical significance with selection stability, we performed 1000 bootstrap resampling iterations; variables with a mean bootstrap score ≥0.4 and a selection probability ≥50% were considered statistically significant and were retained in the final MM-CI score model. β coefficients and hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs were calculated for the final score model, referred to as the MM-CI. For clinical applicability, the β coefficients of predictors in the final model were rounded to integer values. Individual risk estimates were then derived from these weighted scores for each variable. For validation of the MM-CI in Part II, we compared the predictive accuracy of the MM-CI, age-adjusted CCI, and CCI component of the IMWG-frailty score across multiple time points, ranging from 1 to 8 years, using time-dependent Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves. We utilized the time-dependent area under the ROC curve (AUC) at various time intervals, using the R package timeROC . The time-dependent ROC analysis is computed using the inverse probability of censoring weighting, which assigns weights to the cases and controls based on the probability of remaining uncensored, as estimated by the Kaplan–Meier curve [ ]. All statistical analyses were conducted using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA) and R version 4.0.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results Patient characteristics Baseline demographics and clinical characteristics of the development and validation cohorts are summarized in Table . The development cohort ( n = 17,273) comprised 53.7% male patients, with a median age of 63 years (IQR, 53–73). The most common comorbidities in the development cohort were renal disease (22.4%), diabetes (17.1%), cerebrovascular (7.9%). In validation cohort I (Korean registry, n = 1473), patients had a median age of 63 years (IQR, 56–69), with 52.7% male patients. The most common comorbidities were renal disease (29.0%), diabetes (16.0%), and cancer (7.6%). In validation cohort II (Japanese registry, n = 314), patients had a median age of 71 years (IQR, 64–76), with 51.0% male patients. The most common comorbidities were peripheral vascular disease (40.4%), diabetes (18.8%), cancer (14.6%), and congestive heart failure (10.2%). The R2-ISS stage distribution in validation cohort I was 8.4% for stage I, 13.2% for stage II, 23.4% for stage III, and 6.2% for stage IV, with 48.8% of patients missing R2-ISS classification. In validation cohort II, R2-ISS data were available for 72 patients (22.9%), including 2.9% with stage I, 7.3% with stage II, 11.5% with stage III, and 1.3% with stage IV disease. R2-ISS staging was not available for the development cohort due to the limitations of claims data. Median follow-up durations were 66.0 months (95% CI, 64.8–67.6) in the development cohort, 59.6 months (95% CI, 57.3–62.1) in validation cohort I, and 52.0 months (95% CI, 47.8–59.4) in validation cohort II. Corresponding median OS was 41.1 months (95% CI, 40.0–42.0), 84.1 months (95% CI, 76.9–93.6), and 109.0 months (95% CI, 84.9–not reached), respectively (Fig. ). Development of the scoring system (MM-CI) The univariable analysis identified sex, age and 11 comorbidity factors related to poor OS ( p -value < 0.05) in the development cohort (Table ): male (HR 1.09, 95% CI [1.05–1.14]), older age (60–69 years, HR 1.48, 95% CI [1.39–1.57]; 70–79 years, HR 2.26, 95% CI [2.14–2.40]; ≥80 years, HR 3.56, 95% CI [3.31–3.83]), myocardial infarction (HR 1.39, 95% CI [1.18–1.65]), congestive heart failure (HR 1.70, 95% CI [1.56–1.84]), peripheral vascular disease (HR 1.46, 95% CI [1.27–1.67]), cerebrovascular disease (HR 1.40, 95% CI [1.31–1.51]), dementia (HR 1.51, 95% CI [1.27–1.80]), chronic pulmonary disease (HR 1.42, 95% CI [1.30–1.55]), hepatic disease (HR 1.11, 95% CI [1.02–1.22]), diabetes (HR 1.22, 95% CI [1.16–1.29]), hemiplegia/paraplegia (HR 1.42, 95% CI [1.13–1.78]), renal disease (HR 1.16, 95% CI [1.10–1.21]), and cancer (HR 1.23, 95% CI [1.16–1.31]). Multivariable stepwise analysis showed that six variables were significantly associated with poor OS, with all p -values < 0.001 (Table ). Specifically, male sex (HR 1.13,

1.39, 95% CI [1.18–1.65]), congestive heart failure (HR 1.70, 95% CI [1.56–1.84]), peripheral vascular disease (HR 1.46, 95% CI [1.27–1.67]), cerebrovascular disease (HR 1.40, 95% CI [1.31–1.51]), dementia (HR 1.51, 95% CI [1.27–1.80]), chronic pulmonary disease (HR 1.42, 95% CI [1.30–1.55]), hepatic disease (HR 1.11, 95% CI [1.02–1.22]), diabetes (HR 1.22, 95% CI [1.16–1.29]), hemiplegia/paraplegia (HR 1.42, 95% CI [1.13–1.78]), renal disease (HR 1.16, 95% CI [1.10–1.21]), and cancer (HR 1.23, 95% CI [1.16–1.31]). Multivariable stepwise analysis showed that six variables were significantly associated with poor OS, with all p -values < 0.001 (Table ). Specifically, male sex (HR 1.13, 95% CI [1.09–1.18]), advanced age (HR 1.45, 95% CI [1.37–1.54] for ages 60–69; HR 2.20, 95% CI [2.08–2.33] for ages 70–79; HR 3.41, 95% CI [3.17–3.68] for ages ≥80), congestive heart failure (HR 1.46, 95% CI [1.34–1.59]), cerebrovascular disease (HR 1.13, 95% CI [1.05–1.21]), hepatic disease (HR 1.18, 95% CI [1.08–1.29]), and cancer (HR 1.18, 95% CI [1.11–1.26]) were significant predictors. The β coefficients of predictors were rounded to the nearest integer to create a clinically practical scoring system. Risk scores for each predictor were derived as follows: MM-CI score = 1 × (Sex: Male) + 2 × (Age: 60–69 years) + 4 × (Age: 70–79 years) + 6 × (Age ≥80 years) + 2 × (Congestive heart failure: Yes) + 1 × (Cerebrovascular disease: Yes) + 1 × (Hepatic disease: Yes) + 1 × (Cancer: Yes) Application of the MM-CI to the development cohort revealed a clear separation in OS across risk scores (log-rank p < 0.05), as demonstrated by Kaplan–Meier analysis (Fig. ). Using optimal cutoff points determined by recursive partitioning and the median OS estimates, patients were stratified into four risk groups: low risk (0–2 points), intermediate-I (3–4 points), intermediate-II (5 points), and high risk (≥6 points), with corresponding median OS of 72.5 months (95% CI: 69.2–75.0), 43.8 months (95% CI: 42.1–46.3), 30.9 months (95% CI: 28.8–33.2), and 20.3 months (95% CI: 18.9–22.3), respectively (Fig. ). Similarly, MM-CI stratified time to next treatment (log-rank p < 0.05), with median value of 23.4 months (95% CI: 22.6–24.5), 18.5 months (95% CI: 17.9–19.3), 14.8 months (95% CI: 13.9–15.7), and 12.1 months (95% CI: 11.3–13.1) across the four groups, respectively (Fig. ). The model’s internal validity and variable selection stability were confirmed through bootstrap resampling analysis (Table ). Additionally, the MM-CI demonstrated consistent prognostic performance across all frontline treatment intensity groups, supporting its robustness and broad clinical applicability (all p -values < 0.001; Table , Fig. ). Validation of MM-CI The developed MM-CI model was applied to both validation cohort I (Korean registry) and cohort II (Japanese registry). As shown in Fig. , Kaplan–Meier curves revealed significant differences in OS across the four risk groups in both cohorts ( p < 0.001 for each). In validation cohort I, median OS was 97.6 months (95% CI: 92.8–110.9) for the low-risk group, 75.5 months (95% CI: 64.0–94.6) for intermediate-I, 64.5 months (95% CI: 49.7–76.1) for intermediate-II, and 43.0 months (95% CI: 37.2–53.1) for the high-risk group. In validation cohort II, median OS was not reached in the low-risk group; survival estimates were 90.6 months (95% CI: 83.7–not reached) for intermediate-I, 84.9 months (95% CI: 79.1–not reached) for intermediate-II, and 67.8 months (95% CI: 45.3–not reached) for the high-risk group (Fig. ). Predictive accuracy over time was assessed using time-dependent ROC analysis, yielding an integrated AUC of 0.637 (95% CI: 0.610–0.665) when combining both validation cohorts (Fig. ). The MM-CI demonstrated superior discriminative ability compared to the conventional age-adjusted CCI (AUC: 0.613; 95% CI: 0.584–0.641) and the concise age-adjusted CCI used in the IMWG frailty model (AUC: 0.569; 95% CI: 0.546–0.593), with statistically significant differences at most time points ( p < 0.001; Fig. ). Subgroup analysis of MM-CI across ECOG, R2-ISS, and treatment intensity Figures and illustrate HRs and OS across clinical subgroups stratified by the MM-CI risk, demonstrating consistent and stepwise prognostic impact across all strata compared to the low-risk group. Among patients with ECOG performance status of ≤2 ( n = 1437), intermediate-I, intermediate-II, and high-risk groups were associated with HRs of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.11–1.69), 1.88 (95% CI, 1.41–2.49), and 2.27 (95% CI, 1.65–3.11), respectively ( p < 0.001). In those with ECOG ≥ 3 ( n = 264), corresponding HRs were 2.23 (95% CI, 1.50–3.30), 2.05 (95% CI, 1.20–3.51), and 3.12 (95% CI, 1.86–5.24) ( p < 0.001). Prognostic trends were preserved across treatment intensity subgroups. Among patients receiving doublet regimens ( n = 389), HRs for the intermediate-I, intermediate-II, and high-risk groups were 1.69 (95% CI, 1.15–2.47), 2.38 (95% CI, 1.43–3.93), and 3.92 (95% CI, 2.54–6.07), respectively. In patients treated with triplet or quadruplet regimens ( n = 1383), HRs were 1.49 (95% CI, 1.21–1.83), 1.81 (95% CI, 1.36–2.41), and 2.02 (95% CI, 1.42–2.86) ( p <

In those with ECOG ≥ 3 ( n = 264), corresponding HRs were 2.23 (95% CI, 1.50–3.30), 2.05 (95% CI, 1.20–3.51), and 3.12 (95% CI, 1.86–5.24) ( p < 0.001). Prognostic trends were preserved across treatment intensity subgroups. Among patients receiving doublet regimens ( n = 389), HRs for the intermediate-I, intermediate-II, and high-risk groups were 1.69 (95% CI, 1.15–2.47), 2.38 (95% CI, 1.43–3.93), and 3.92 (95% CI, 2.54–6.07), respectively. In patients treated with triplet or quadruplet regimens ( n = 1383), HRs were 1.49 (95% CI, 1.21–1.83), 1.81 (95% CI, 1.36–2.41), and 2.02 (95% CI, 1.42–2.86) ( p < 0.001 for both subgroups). R2-ISS–based stratification showed similarly consistent gradients. In patients with stage I/II disease ( n = 350), the intermediate-I, intermediate-II, and high-risk groups had HRs of 2.69 (95% CI, 1.50–4.83), 3.33 (95% CI, 1.52–7.33), and 3.63 (95% CI, 1.65–7.97), respectively. In those with stage III/IV disease ( n = 476), corresponding HRs were 1.68 (95% CI, 1.19–2.37), 1.79 (95% CI, 1.10–2.93), and 2.84 (95% CI, 1.71–4.73), respectively ( p < 0.001 for all). In multivariable analysis (Table and Fig. ), the MM-CI retained its independent prognostic value after adjustment for ECOG performance status, frontline treatment intensity, and R2-ISS stage. Adjusted HRs for the intermediate-I, intermediate-II, and high-risk MM-CI groups were 1.95 (95% CI, 1.44–2.64), 2.07 (95% CI, 1.36–3.16), and 2.75 (95% CI, 1.78–4.25), respectively ( p < 0.001 for all). Among covariates, both R2-ISS stage and ECOG performance status remained significant predictors of OS ( p < 0.05), while frontline treatment intensity did not show a statistically significant association with survival (adjusted p = 0.156). Web-based application for score model The developed MM-CI scoring system was implemented in an R script, and a web-based R Shiny application was developed to facilitate clinical use. The application is freely available at ( https://pipetapp.com/project/mm_survival/ ) and provides clinicians with an intuitive interface for calculating patient-specific survival risk. Figure demonstrates the application interface and functionality. Discussion We developed a comorbidity-based MM risk model, termed the MM-CI, by integrating patient-related factors—including male sex, advanced age, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, hepatic disease, and prior cancer—using data from a nationwide Korean claims database (HIRA). This model was externally validated in two independent real-world cohorts from Korea and Japan, and demonstrated robust prognostic performance independent of established clinical risk factors, including ECOG performance status, frontline treatment intensity, and cytogenetic abnormalities defined by the R2-ISS framework. The MM-CI outperformed the conventional CCI model and concise CCI-based model derived from the IMWG frailty score, which was developed exclusively from clinical trial populations and has limited real-world validation despite widespread clinical adoption [ ]. Our model addresses this gap by leveraging multivariate modeling and real-world data to generate a streamlined, statistically robust, and clinically applicable comorbidity index. Although the CCI has been widely used to quantify comorbidity burden and predict survival, its application in MM is limited. First, it was originally developed to estimate short-term mortality in general medical populations and may not capture the chronic course of hematologic malignancies such as MM [ ]. Second, its weighting scheme is static and does not account for disease-specific relevance or population heterogeneity [ ]. Third, it fails to reflect advances in treatment and prognostic paradigms that have emerged over recent decades [ , ]. In response, alternative models such as the IMWG frailty score and the Revised Myeloma Comorbidity Index (R-MCI) have been proposed. The R-MCI incorporates variables such as renal and lung function, frailty scores, and age [ ]. While these models offer enhanced precision, their implementation can be time-consuming and may require functional assessments not routinely available in clinical practice. Moreover, the R-MCI was developed using prospectively enrolled clinical trial populations, which typically exclude patients with severe comorbidities through strict eligibility criteria. As a result, these models may underrepresent patients with severe comorbidities—precisely those who pose the greatest clinical challenge in the real world. In contrast, our model was derived from a nationwide real-world cohort of 17,273 patients and validated in a multi-institutional setting across two countries. This approach allowed inclusion of patients with a broader spectrum of comorbidities—particularly those often underrepresented in trials. The model was developed through rigorous multivariate selection from 13 candidate variables known to influence survival in MM. Six final predictors—male sex, advanced age, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, hepatic disease, and prior cancer—were independently associated with OS. Several of these variables (e.g., congestive heart failure and prior cancer) are commonly used as exclusion criteria in clinical trials but are frequently encountered in practice. Notably, although renal disease was the most prevalent comorbidity (22.4%) and retained statistical significance in full models, its incremental prognostic contribution was limited after accounting for age and overlapping cardiorenal and vascular conditions. As such, it did not meet the threshold for inclusion in the final simplified MM-CI

known to influence survival in MM. Six final predictors—male sex, advanced age, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, hepatic disease, and prior cancer—were independently associated with OS. Several of these variables (e.g., congestive heart failure and prior cancer) are commonly used as exclusion criteria in clinical trials but are frequently encountered in practice. Notably, although renal disease was the most prevalent comorbidity (22.4%) and retained statistical significance in full models, its incremental prognostic contribution was limited after accounting for age and overlapping cardiorenal and vascular conditions. As such, it did not meet the threshold for inclusion in the final simplified MM-CI scoring system. This finding highlights the value of real-world data in building inclusive, generalizable risk models. Time-dependent ROC analysis demonstrated that the MM-CI consistently outperformed both the conventional age-adjusted CCI and the concise CCI used in the IMWG frailty score across all time points. Moreover, its prognostic value remained significant after adjusting for ECOG status, treatment intensity, and R2-ISS—underscoring its utility as an independent risk tool. However, our study has limitations. First, the HIRA dataset does not capture functional assessments such as ADL or IADL, which are important but difficult to standardize in real-world settings. Moreover, comorbidities in the development cohort were ascertained from administrative ICD‑10 codes in a claims database, which may under‑ or over‑estimate the true burden of some conditions despite the use of validated coding algorithms and stringent confirmation rules. External validation in registry‑based cohorts partially mitigates this concern but does not fully eliminate the possibility of misclassification. Second, because the MM-CI was developed in a Korean nationwide cohort and validated in Korean and Japanese registry cohorts, additional studies are needed to confirm its generalizability in other ethnic groups and healthcare systems. Third, median OS differed substantially between the nationwide claims-based development cohort and the Korean and Japanese registry-based validation cohorts. This discrepancy likely reflects differences in calendar period, treatment intensity and access to novel agents, as well as referral and selection inherent to tertiary academic centers. Additionally, registry datasets may be subject to administrative censoring or incomplete death ascertainment, whereas the HIRA database includes linkage to national mortality records, enabling more accurate survival estimation. Therefore, the MM-CI is best applied for within-cohort risk stratification, and absolute survival comparisons across cohorts should be interpreted with caution. Finally, our cohorts were accrued largely during an era dominated by proteasome inhibitor- and IMiD-based doublet and triplet regimens, with the more recent introduction of quadruplets, and had limited exposure to CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates. Extrapolation of the MM-CI to modern immunotherapy-based strategies should therefore be cautious and will require prospective validation in immunotherapy-treated populations. In conclusion, the MM-CI provides a simple, objective, and statistically robust comorbidity-based risk score that is readily applicable in routine practice. It adds independent prognostic information beyond R2-ISS, ECOG performance status and treatment intensity, and may help tailor real-world treatment decisions, including transplant eligibility and the choice between doublet, triplet, or quadruplet frontline regimens. Future studies—particularly in cohorts receiving CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies, or antibody–drug conjugate-containing regimens—are warranted to test, refine, and, if necessary, recalibrate the MM-CI for contemporary immunotherapy-based treatment strategies. chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is the most common acute leukemia in adults [ ] occurring in 4.3 in 100 000 individuals in the United States [ ]. AML is a heterogeneous disease with numerous cytogenetic and molecular features influencing prognosis [ , , ]. According to current guidelines, accurate diagnosis and initial evaluation of AML requires clinical, morphological, cytogenetic, and molecular genetic assessment [ , , , ]. Approximately 50% of patients with AML have an abnormal karyotype, and a median of 3 gene mutations per patient [ ]. More mutations are generally associated with worse prognosis; however, prognosis depends heavily on which genes are mutated [ ]. The addition of diagnostic molecular genetic testing results to risk stratification models has enhanced prognostication [ , ] and, with the advent of targeted therapies, has become essential in making treatment decisions. Since 2017, four targeted therapies have been approved for treatment of AML: the FLT3 inhibitors midostaurin [ , ] and gilteritinib [ ] for newly diagnosed and relapsed/refractory patients, respectively, the IDH1 inhibitor ivosidenib [ , , ] for newly diagnosed and relapsed/refractory patients, and the IDH2 inhibitor enasidenib [ ] for relapsed/refractory patients. Enasidenib was evaluated in patients with newly diagnosed IDH2 + AML [ ], and sorafenib and dasatinib are used off‐label for patients with FLT3‐ITD and KIT mutations, respectively [ , ]. Quizartinib and crenolanib are FLT3 inhibitors under clinical investigation [ , ], as is FT‐2102 for IDH1 [ ] and APR‐246 for TP53 [ ]. Despite the critical roles that diagnostic and molecular genetic testing play in AML treatment [ ], our understanding of how these tests are used, particularly in older patients who are often excluded from clinical trials, is limited. Outcomes in older patients with AML remain poor; median survival ranges from 2.5 to 24.5 months, depending on risk group [ , ]. Several factors contribute to poor outcomes, including an increased probability of drug resistance and unfavorable cytogenetics [ ]. Older patients often receive less intensive therapy due to perceived frailty, which can lead to worse outcomes [ , ]. We summarize diagnostic and molecular testing patterns by site, enrolment year, and adherence to guidelines in patients with AML enrolled in the Connect ® MDS/AML Disease Registry. 2 MATERIALS AND METHODS 2.1 Study design and setting The Connect ® MDS/AML Disease Registry is a large, ongoing, US, multicenter, prospective observational cohort study of patients with newly diagnosed AML, MDS, or idiopathic cytopenia of undetermined significance ( NCT01688011 ). A full description of the study design and objectives was reported previously [ ]. The study is non‐interventional; all medical care is performed at the discretion of the treating clinicians in accordance with standard clinical practice at each site. The Registry was approved by a central institutional review board (IRB; Advarra Review IRB, Seattle, WA, USA) or the IRB at each site. All patients provided written informed consent. Enrolment began in December 2013 and will continue until approximately 2100 patients have enrolled, including 700 patients with AML, from approximately 150 to 200 sites. 2.2 Participants To minimize selection bias, consecutive patients with AML seen at participating sites are invited to enrol in the Registry. Patients aged ≥55 years and newly diagnosed with primary or secondary AML, as per the 2008 revised World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines [ ], within 60 days of enrolment are eligible. Local diagnosis is confirmed by independent central pathology review of laboratory reports. Bone marrow (BM) aspirate and biopsy results are not required if laboratory results indicate ≥20% myeloblasts in the peripheral blood. Patients are excluded if they have suspected or diagnosed acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). Patients with AML are also excluded if they have received active, disease‐modifying treatment for ≥14 days prior to enrolment. Patients receiving only supportive care may enroll. 2.3 Measurements Patient data are collected in an electronic data capture system at baseline and every 3 months for up to 8 years, or until early study termination, patient withdrawal, or death. Data include patient characteristics, comorbidities (assessed by the Adult Comorbidity Evaluation form ACE‐27 [ ], frailty evaluation (assessed by the Canadian Study of Health and Aging [CSHA] Clinical Frailty Scale [ , ]), diagnostic testing results, treatment, and outcomes. Molecular genetic testing data presented are based on the 19 genes (Figure S1) included in the study electronic database. 2.4 Statistical analyses Demographics and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Categorical values were reported as proportions of the total Registry cohort. P‐ values were calculated for pairwise comparisons of baseline variables at academic and community/government sites using chi‐square test, Fisher exact test (for categorical values) and Wilcoxon test (for median values). Factors associated with molecular genetic testing of 19 specific mutations were evaluated using univariate and multivariable logistic regression analysis with variable selection based

testing results, treatment, and outcomes. Molecular genetic testing data presented are based on the 19 genes (Figure S1) included in the study electronic database. 2.4 Statistical analyses Demographics and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Categorical values were reported as proportions of the total Registry cohort. P‐ values were calculated for pairwise comparisons of baseline variables at academic and community/government sites using chi‐square test, Fisher exact test (for categorical values) and Wilcoxon test (for median values). Factors associated with molecular genetic testing of 19 specific mutations were evaluated using univariate and multivariable logistic regression analysis with variable selection based on chi‐square statistics. Variables significant at P < .1 in univariate analyses were included in multivariable analyses. All statistical analyses were conducted using SAS ® version 9.2 or higher (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA). Statistical testing was conducted at an α = .05 (two‐sided) significance level. The data cut‐off for this analysis was 8 March 2019. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Baseline characteristics Baseline characteristics and testing data collected from patients enrolled in the Registry from 12 December 2013 to the data cut‐off (8 March 2019) were included in this analysis. In total, 565 patients with newly diagnosed AML were enrolled in the Registry across 116 sites in the US (Table ). Median age was 70 years (range 55–92 years) and 72.7% were aged ≥65 years. A total of 229 patients (40.5%) were enrolled from academic sites and 336 (59.5%) from community/government sites. Academic centers in the Northeast and South enrolled most patients, and community/government sites more commonly enrolled patients in the Midwest and South. Most patients had an ECOG PS of 0‐1 (72.5%) and a mild (1‐4) CSHA Clinical Frailty Scale score (84.2%). About 40% of patients had an ACE‐27 comorbidity score of 2‐3. 3.2 Bone marrow blast assessment and morphology BM blast percentage was reported for 82.1% of patients. BM blasts were measured by a manual count from the aspirate or touch preparation in 71.7% of patients (Figure ), as recommended by the WHO guidelines [ , ]. Cellularity was the most commonly reported BM morphological feature, assessed in 93.6% of patients. Dysplasia was reported in 42.4‐62.9% of patients, fibrosis in 44.2% of patients, and ring sideroblasts in 52.4% of patients (Table ). 3.3 Ancillary testing, including molecular genetic testing Conventional karyotyping, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) were reported in 95.4%, 98.8%, and 75.7% of patients, respectively. Molecular genetic testing was reported in 429 patients (75.9%) (Table ) and was done more frequently at academic than community/government sites (84.3% vs 70.2%; P = .0001). Only 3.2% of patients underwent FISH or molecular genetic testing without conventional karyotyping. Of 429 patients who underwent molecular testing, blood specimens were analyzed for 89 patients and BM for 346 patients (Table ). Median time from sample collection to reporting of molecular testing results for both blood and BM samples was 7 days. The time from BM sample collection to reporting of the results was longer for patients enrolled later in the Registry (2017‐2019), versus those enrolled earlier (2013‐2016; 8.5 vs 7 days, respectively; P = .007). For blood samples no significant difference in turnaround time was observed. There was variability in the number of genes tested (median 4, interquartile range [IQR: 3–17] from a total of 19 genes listed in Figure S1; Figure ). The most frequently tested mutations were FLT3‐ITD (87.9%), NPM1 (79.7%), FLT3‐TKD (77.9%), and CEBPA (61.1%), consistent with National Comprehensive Cancer Network © (NCCN) molecular testing recommendations [ ] (Figure S1). At academic sites, univariate analysis identified five factors associated with molecular genetic testing: enrolment year, geographic region, age, normal karyotype, and European Leukemia Network (ELN) risk score. In multivariable analysis, factors significantly associated with higher testing rates were residing in the Northeast versus "Other" regions (odds ratio [OR] 16.13; 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.11 to 125.00; P = .007), normal karyotype (OR 3.01; 95% CI 1.20‐7.52; P = .018), and enrolment in 2017‐2019 versus earlier enrolment (OR 2.59; 95% CI 1.14‐5.88; P = .023) (Figure ). At community/government sites, univariate analysis identified seven factors associated with molecular genetic testing: enrolment year, region, age, insurance type, normal karyotype, ELN risk score, and comorbidity score. In multivariable analysis, factors significantly associated with higher testing rates included enrolment in 2017‐2019 versus earlier enrolment (OR 4.85; 95% CI 2.25‐10.53; P < .001), a favorable or intermediate ELN risk score vs adverse risk score (OR 3.45; 95% CI 1.77‐6.71; P < .001), and age < 65 years vs ≥65 years (OR 2.80; 95% CI 1.138‐6.891; P = .025). The only overlapping independent predictor of molecular testing at both academic and community/government sites was enrolment year (Figure ). 3.4 Conformity with molecular genetic tests recommended in the ASH/CAP guidelines Figure summarizes adherence to the American Society of Hematology/College of American Pathologists (ASH/CAP) guidelines

significantly associated with higher testing rates included enrolment in 2017‐2019 versus earlier enrolment (OR 4.85; 95% CI 2.25‐10.53; P < .001), a favorable or intermediate ELN risk score vs adverse risk score (OR 3.45; 95% CI 1.77‐6.71; P < .001), and age < 65 years vs ≥65 years (OR 2.80; 95% CI 1.138‐6.891; P = .025). The only overlapping independent predictor of molecular testing at both academic and community/government sites was enrolment year (Figure ). 3.4 Conformity with molecular genetic tests recommended in the ASH/CAP guidelines Figure summarizes adherence to the American Society of Hematology/College of American Pathologists (ASH/CAP) guidelines [ ], which recommend several molecular genetic tests for patients with AML. The guidelines strongly recommend FLT3‐ITD testing for all patients with AML; this was performed in 87.9% of the 429 patients who received molecular testing. Recommended testing was also reported for TET2 (34.0%), WT1 (29.6%), IDH1 (46.6%), IDH2 (46.6%), DNMT3A (35.9%), and TP53 (34.3%). Of the 278 patients without myelodysplastic cytogenetic abnormalities, APL or core binding factor (CBF)‐AML who received molecular testing, testing for NPM1 , CEBPA , and RUNX1 was reported in 80.9%, 60.1%, and 31.3% of patients, respectively. Of the 22 patients with CBF‐AML who underwent molecular testing, KIT was assessed in 18 (81.8%) patients. 3.5 Changes in molecular genetic testing over time To assess if testing patterns have changed since 2013, we compared the mutations tested in patients enrolled early in the Registry (2013‐2016) with those enrolled later (2017‐2019), after the first targeted therapy in AML was approved. These timepoints reflect the publication of updated diagnostic guidelines [ , , ]. In patients enrolled in 2013‐2016, 57.1% of testing used PCR and 35.3% used next‐generation sequencing (NGS), versus 52.6% for PCR and 39.2% for NGS in 2017‐2019. Of the 19 genes analyzed by molecular testing, the mean number of mutations tested for patients enrolled in 2013‐2016 was 6 versus 10 in 2017‐2019 ( P < .001). Testing rates for individual mutations generally increased between 2013 and 2019 (Figure ). The largest increases were for IDH1 and IDH2 (Figure ), for which the targeted therapies ivosidenib and enasidenib, respectively, were approved in the United States in 2019 and 2017. We also assessed how the use of targeted therapies changed over the duration of the Registry to date. Of 24 patients who received targeted therapies (midostaurin, ivosidenib, enasidenib, sorafenib, or gilteritinib) in 2013–2016, 6 (25.0%) received midostaurin and 18 (75.0%) received sorafenib. Given the 2017 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of enasidenib and the 2018 approval of ivosidenib and gilteritinib, no patients received these drugs before 2017. Of 53 patients who received targeted therapies in 2017‐2019, one (1.9%) received ivosidenib, seven (13.2%) received enasidenib, 20 (37.7%) received midostaurin, 24 (45.3%) received sorafenib, and one (1.9%) received gilteritinib (Table ). Of 59 patients with mutant IDH1 or IDH2 , one (1.7%) received ivosidenib and four (6.8%) received enasidenib. Of 88 patients with either FLT3‐ITD or FLT3‐TKD mutations, 12 (13.6%) received midostaurin, one (1.4%) received gilteritinib, and 24 (27.2%) received sorafenib. Eighty‐one patients received an investigational drug; 45 enrolled in 2013‐2016, and 36 enrolled in 2017‐2019. 4 DISCUSSION This analysis from the Connect ® MDS/AML Disease Registry suggests that, in a clinical practice setting outside of a clinical trial, physicians largely follow testing guidelines, although there is a need for further education to increase testing rates. In this study, blast assessment was performed manually in 71.7% of Registry patients. The WHO guidelines recommend that blast percentages should be determined manually using 200‐cell leucocyte differential counts of the peripheral blood, and 500‐cell differential counts of all nucleated BM cells in cellular marrow aspirate smears stained with Wright‐Giemsa [ , ]. A low rate of manual differentials may indicate poor aspirates rather than a lack of awareness of the WHO guidelines. For poor quality aspirates immunohistochemistry may be useful; however, use of flow cytometry to determine blast percentage by counting CD34 + cells is discouraged because not all leukemic blasts express CD34, and hemodilution and processing artifacts can cause inaccurate estimation of blast percentage [ , ]. In a physician survey, respondents reported routinely using flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, and karyotyping with poor quality aspirates [ ]. Molecular testing patterns in AML varied depending on several factors, including patient age, karyotype, treatment setting, and geographic region. Older patients were less likely to undergo molecular testing at community/government sites versus academic sites; similar results were reported in a smaller retrospective study evaluating molecular testing rates in patients with AML [ ], where molecular testing was performed in 93% of patients diagnosed at academic centers and 41% of patients diagnosed at outside centers ( P < .001). This observation may reflect the availability of testing, differences in cooperation between clinical and laboratory experts [ ], increased testing as a requirement for clinical trial

AML varied depending on several factors, including patient age, karyotype, treatment setting, and geographic region. Older patients were less likely to undergo molecular testing at community/government sites versus academic sites; similar results were reported in a smaller retrospective study evaluating molecular testing rates in patients with AML [ ], where molecular testing was performed in 93% of patients diagnosed at academic centers and 41% of patients diagnosed at outside centers ( P < .001). This observation may reflect the availability of testing, differences in cooperation between clinical and laboratory experts [ ], increased testing as a requirement for clinical trial enrolment at academic centers, or bias that older patients are unlikely to benefit from therapy [ ]. It is increasingly acknowledged that age should not be the only factor in making treatment decisions [ ], partially because novel, targeted therapies may be better tolerated than conventional therapies. This may lead to an increase in molecular testing rates in older patients. Multivariable analyses revealed that the only overlapping predictor for molecular testing at both academic and community/government sites was enrolment after 2016. This may suggest changing diagnostic practices as AML testing guidelines were updated [ , , ]. The observation that patients with a normal karyotype were more likely to undergo molecular testing may be due to the perception that molecular genetic testing has a higher yield in normal karyotype patients, dating from an era when guidelines only recommended molecular testing in such patients; now, with the ability to therapeutically target specific mutations, molecular testing has a larger role than simply prognostication. It may also reflect economic factors, reserving costly molecular testing for patients most likely to need accurate risk assessment. The increase in molecular testing rates for individual genes may be explained by growing awareness of how specific mutations impact survival, and/or by the approval of new targeted therapies. Midostaurin was approved for use in 2017 after being shown to prolong survival for newly diagnosed AML patients with an FLT3 mutation [ ]. Our data show that FLT3 testing rates have increased since the publication of these data and drug approval. Similarly, testing rates for IDH2 have increased since enasidenib was approved as a targeted therapy in 2017 [ ]. While more patients enrolled in the Registry in 2017‐2019 received targeted therapies versus those enrolled in 2013‐2016, overall molecular testing rates are low when national guideline recommendations are considered. This could be because several drugs, including midostaurin, enasidenib, and ivosidenib, have only recently been approved for first‐line treatment [ , , ]. As the Registry continues to enroll patients, it will be possible to monitor how recently approved agents are introduced into clinical practice. We noted wide variations in the mutations being tested, revealing the heterogeneity of panels used at different sites. A standardized panel including guideline‐suggested genes may ensure patients are tested for actionable mutations (eg, FLT3 , IDH2 ) and identify patients eligible for clinical trials and treatment with targeted therapies. The development of a standardized testing panel presents several challenges including: the choice of hotspots/mutations included; variant allele frequency selected; quality and reproducibility of the panel; and financial cost, including insurance reimbursement [ , ]. The Registry does not capture reasons that may explain the differences in diagnostic approach among treatment sites. Differences in access to testing services, costs of testing, and variations in insurance reimbursements may influence testing patterns. Results may also change as more patients with AML enroll in the Registry. An increase in molecular testing was already seen over a relatively short period of time, and testing frequency may continue to change, particularly as guidelines are updated or new targeted therapies become available. One important strength of this Registry study is that it represents current routine clinical practice for newly diagnosed patients with AML across practice settings. There were few eligibility criteria other than age (≥55 years) and no comorbidity restrictions. Therefore, the data presented here closely reflect the older patients’ experience. As with all studies using data from routine clinical practice, this study was subject to limitations concerning lack of randomization and specific protocols for patient assessment and intervention. Despite this, the Registry represents one of the largest prospective cohort studies of patients with AML, treated in geographically diverse and mainly community‐based settings in the United States, and provides insights into their clinical experience. Regardless of the as‐yet‐unknown prognostic value of molecular testing [ , ], the advent of targeted therapies for AML underscores the importance of molecular characterization of AML in all patients. Introduction The optimal intensity of treatment in adults who are frail with multiple myeloma (MM) is often uncertain, given the higher risk of harm in patients who are frail on standard, intensive regimens. , Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) directly or indirectly exclude patients who are frail, limiting the generalizability of results to a large portion of patients treated in practice. , Although analyses from RCTs and observational studies consistently show that frailty is associated with higher risks of treatment toxicity, treatment discontinuation, and mortality, this evidence does little to inform the key clinical question, that is, whether to administer to patients who are frail, in practice, the same intensity of treatments evaluated in the younger, fitter patients in RCTs. An illustrative example is Southwest Oncology Group (SWOG) S0777, the seminal randomized phase 3 trial that demonstrated an overall survival benefit associated with a more intensive triplet (bortezomib-lenalidomide-dexamethasone or VRd) vs a less intensive doublet (lenalidomide-dexamethasone or Rd) regimen in patients newly diagnosed with MM not intended for immediate hematopoietic stem cell transplant. These findings solidified the recommendation to favor initiation on the triplet VRd over the doublet Rd in most patients. However, many experts and guidelines have historically recommended Rd over VRd for patients who are frail and may not be able to tolerate a triplet. , To date, there has been no evidence suggesting that patients who are frail treated with VRd experience either lesser benefits and/or greater harms than those treated with Rd. Although there are newer triplet regimens that are preferred in older patients (eg, daratumumab-lenalidomide-dexamethasone ), examining the effects of VRd vs Rd provides an opportunity to examine whether patients who are frail, in practice, fare worse on a more intensive initial regimen. We designed a retrospective cohort study in US veterans, a population that is even more underrepresented in MM clinical trials than the general population, to evaluate for differences in survival associated with VRd vs Rd in newly diagnosed MM. We hypothesized that, similar to the results of SWOG S0777, we would observe a survival benefit associated with VRd over Rd in the overall population. Furthermore, we hypothesized that, similar to assumptions behind expert recommendations for clinical practice, the survival benefit associated with VRd would diminish in patients with high levels of frailty than in relatively fit patients, whereas the risk of hospitalization would increase (reflecting higher toxicity). Methods Study design and population Emulating SWOG S0777, we designed a retrospective cohort study using a new-user design that uses data from the Veterans Affairs (VA) Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW), which collects clinical, billing, and electronic health record (EHR) information from veterans treated in VA facilities throughout the United States. We also used data from the national VA Cancer Registry, which collects information on cancer diagnosis and treatment compiled and submitted by local cancer registry staff at each of the 132 VA Medical Centers that diagnose and treat veterans with cancer. , Using a selection algorithm validated against clinician chart review, we included all veterans newly diagnosed with MM who initiated treatment in VA Medical centers with either VRd or Rd from years 2004 (date of the first instance of using Rd) to 2020 (see regarding our selection algorithm). We excluded veterans who received transplant within the first four months of treatment initiation. Although we could not measure a clinician’s intention to transplant at the time of initiation of VRd or Rd, as was measured in SWOG S0777, we measured the receipt of transplant at any point during follow-up. This study was approved by the VA Boston Health Care System Institutional Review Board. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Frailty, MM stage, and covariates We measured frailty using the Veterans Affairs Frailty Index (VA-FI), an electronic frailty index developed by geriatricians that carries both predictive and construct validity, including when validated against clinical measures of frailty assessed by geriatricians and the International Myeloma Working Group Frailty Score ( ). , , In brief, the VA-FI measures frailty based on the deficit-accumulation approach, which is one of the most widely-studied models of frailty. A total of 31 aging-related health deficits were measured from the EHR data and administrative claims, using diagnostic and procedural codes spanning the domains of morbidity (14 deficits), function (8), cognition (3), sensory (3), and other (3). These health deficits were measured within a 3-year assessment period leading up to the date of treatment initiation. A score was calculated, for each patient, as the proportion of possible health deficits that are present in an individual, ranging from 0 to 1, in which higher values indicate more severe frailty. Based on validated cut-points, , , , , , veterans were classified as nonfrail (VA-FI < 0.2), mildly frail (VA-FI = 0.2-0.3), or moderate-severely frail (VA-FI ≥ 0.3). We measured MM
