chunks.content: Background Aging is associated with a decline of many physiologic functions, determined by factors that include genetic predisposition, environmental influences, and lifestyle choices. However, there is considerable variation in the impact of aging on individual responses to disease [ ]. In cardiovascular medicine, the number and severity of risk factors increases in the elderly, leading to a higher incidence of diseases such as atrial fibrillation (AF), along with sequelae such as systemic thromboembolism and stroke [ ]. The interaction of the body with therapeutic measures changes too, as reflected by altered pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics [ ], associated with changes in glomerular filtration rate, decreased protein binding and decrease in liver function. Therefore, in therapies that cover a wide range of ages, it is prudent to investigate the benefits and risks stratified by age groups [ ]. Based on US data from 2002 [ ], an adult undergoes an average of approximately nine surgical procedures in a lifetime, with a rate that increases with age, reaching a rate of 0.16 operations/person/year at age 75. With over 33 million patients with AF (2010 data) globally [ ], there is a large population at need of oral anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events. An estimated 10% of patients treated with oral anticoagulants are annually subjected to diagnostic or therapeutic procedures [ ] of varying invasiveness and, thus, to the risk of severe bleeding and ischemic events [ ]. All procedures with a bleeding risk require optimization of the peri-procedural management of anticoagulation: whether to interrupt oral anticoagulation at all and if so, for how long and when, relative to the procedure. As patients of advanced age, especially the very elderly aged 85 years and above [ ] are often undertreated with oral anticoagulants because of concerns with regard to increased bleeding risk, and lack of benefit in stroke prevention [ , ]. It is valuable to understand whether older patients are also treated differently peri-procedurally from younger patients. The EMIT (Edoxaban Management in Diagnostic and Therapeutic Procedures) study [ ] prospectively investigated the peri-procedural management and outcome in a large cohort of unselected patients who were treated with the direct oral anticoagulant edoxaban for any of its approved indications. Adding to the EMIT results, this paper discusses the safety and efficacy of edoxaban in elderly patients from those aged ≥ 65 years of age to the very elderly, aged 85 years. Although the majority of patients with AF are elderly, and so typical patient management might be assumed to meet the needs of the elderly, a detailed cohort analysis allows understanding of when, as aging progresses, differences in risk and tactics for treatment and risk mitigation become identifiable. Methods Design The EMIT study was a multicentre, prospective, and noninterventional study integrating data from seven European and four Asian countries. The detailed design has been published [ , ]. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with local Institutional Review Board approvals and was registered as NCT02950168 . Written informed consent was obtained from participants prior to enrolment. The peri-procedural management of anticoagulant therapy was at the discretion of the investigator, including any decision whether to interrupt edoxaban therapy and the timing/duration of any interruption. No attempt was made to influence patient management by the study authors, study team or the sponsor. Objectives and outcome parameters The objective of the registry was to analyse the peri-procedural management of patients receiving edoxaban in daily practice and to collect data on safety and other outcome parameters in these patients. The primary safety outcome was the rate of major bleeding (MB) from five days prior to the procedure to 30 days post-procedure using the International Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) definition [ ]. Secondary outcomes included exploration of the main efficacy outcome, defined as the composite of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), systemic embolic events (SEE), deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), and cardiovascular (CV) mortality, along with the individual components. Other secondary outcomes included the incidences of clinically relevant non-major bleeding (CRNMB) and all-cause mortality. CRNMB events were defined as overt bleeding that required medical attention but that did not fulfil the criteria for MB. Other secondary outcomes of the study were evaluation of the peri-procedural interruption and dosing of edoxaban. All incidents of MB, CRNMB, ACS, and acute thromboembolic events were reviewed and unanimously adjudicated by the Steering Committee. Bleeding had to commence during or after the procedure to be classified as a procedural complication. Patient recruitment Enrolment commenced in December 2016. Subjects were recruited consecutively. Eligible patients were ≥ 18 years of age, had AF, were treated with edoxaban according to the local labels, were not enrolled in any other study concurrently, and underwent any type of diagnostic

fulfil the criteria for MB. Other secondary outcomes of the study were evaluation of the peri-procedural interruption and dosing of edoxaban. All incidents of MB, CRNMB, ACS, and acute thromboembolic events were reviewed and unanimously adjudicated by the Steering Committee. Bleeding had to commence during or after the procedure to be classified as a procedural complication. Patient recruitment Enrolment commenced in December 2016. Subjects were recruited consecutively. Eligible patients were ≥ 18 years of age, had AF, were treated with edoxaban according to the local labels, were not enrolled in any other study concurrently, and underwent any type of diagnostic or therapeutic procedure. Data from the first procedure in each patient is reported. Observations The observation period of the study started five days before the procedure and ended 30 days afterward. Date of visit, details of edoxaban treatment, and clinical outcomes were documented at 30 days after each procedure. No interruption of edoxaban therapy was defined if edoxaban was administered on each day of the observation period. Any interruption of edoxaban treatment was recorded as the number of days without administration of edoxaban, pre-procedural and/or post-procedural. Any dose skipped before or on the day of the procedure was defined as pre-procedural. Peri-procedural EHRA bleeding risk [ ]; HAS-BLED [ ] (Hypertension, Abnormal renal/liver function, Stroke, Bleeding history or predisposition, Labile international normalized ratio, Elderly, Drugs/alcohol concomitantly) score; CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc (Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Age ≥ 75 [doubled], Diabetes, Stroke [doubled]-Vascular disease, Age 65–74 years, and gender [female]) score [ ]; details of edoxaban treatment; diagnostic/therapeutic procedures; and clinical findings were documented at baseline and during the peri-procedural period. Statistical analysis Binary, categorical, and ordinal parameters were summarized by means of absolute and percentage numbers. Numerical data were described by standard statistics. The statistical analyses were performed using SAS ® version 9.3 or higher (SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina, USA). In order to maximize the utility of the data, three sets of age cut-offs were utilized: less than 65 years versus 65 years and older; less than 75 years versus 75 years and older; a more granular set of four groups with < 65, ≥ 65 to < 75, ≥ 75 to < 85, and ≥ 85 years following UN standards [ ]; and in line with the FDA [ ], a second cut-off of 75 years and above was chosen. These multiple cut-offs permit analysis following both conventional definitions of the elderly and very elderly, as well as acknowledging that many populations are reaching advanced age in a healthier state than previous generations [ ]. Use of multiple narrow cohorts, plus their larger combinations, permits analysis whatever definition of the elderly is chosen. Results The dataset included 1,442 patients’ first procedures. Of these patients, 280 (19%) were younger than 65 years, 550 (38%) were 65–74 years old, 514 (36%) 75–84 years old, and 98 (7%) were 85 years old or older. See Fig. . In all age groups except those ≥ 85 years, the patients were predominantly male with the male proportion declining with age. All recorded comorbidities were more prevalent with increasing age, except obesity/overweight (assessed as BMI [ ]) and dyslipidaemia, which trended lower in patients aged 85 years and older. A creatinine clearance of ≤ 50 mL/min was found in 21% of patients aged from 75 to 85 years, and 49% of patients of 85 years or older. Use of the 30 mg edoxaban dose increased with age, being utilized in 9% of patients < 65 years, and in 68% of patients ≥ 85 years. Heparin bridging was used in about 10% of patients, with a slight trend toward greater use in the more elderly. HAS-BLED and CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc scores also increased with age, particularly in the over 75 age groups, (although it should be noted that age is a component of each score). Due to likely correlations among predictors, a stepwise approach is applied. A significance level of 0.1 was set to allow a variable into the model and for a variable to stay in the model. The final selected model includes predictors of weight (p = 0.003), prior coronary heart disease (p = 0.029), prior use of heparin (p = 0.043), and prior use of P-gp inhibitors (p = 0.054). Weight, prior coronary heart disease, and prior use of heparin emerged as independent predictors. EHRA procedural bleeding risk distribution was similar across all age groups, although the proportion of minor risk procedures increased in older age groups. In all patient age groups, vascular access and transcatheter diagnostics or interventions were the most frequently performed procedures. The next three most common procedures across all age groups were cardiovascular/vascular, gastroenterological, and dentistry procedures. Orthopaedic and ophthalmologic procedures were more common in those aged 75 years or more. See Table for further details. Of 1,442 first procedures, 1,324 (92%) were pre-scheduled. Edoxaban was discontinued pre-procedurally in 48% of all patients. Interruption rates were higher and duration of interruption longer in the older age groups. See Table for details. Most patients aged 65 years or more had a post-procedural therapy interruption. Interruptions of two or more days were more common in patients aged 65 years or older (p < 0.001). Figure shows the number of patients in each age group taking edoxaban on each peri-procedural day. Bleeding occurred in 3.9% of patients < 65 years and 4.1% in those 85 years or older. Major bleeding and CRNMB had an overall incidence of 1.0%, with the highest incidence in patients aged 65–74 years (1.6%). There was no discernible relationship between age and all bleeding complications. However, ischemic/thromboembolic complications were more common in the elderly, with all of nine events occurring in those over 65 years, and seven (77.8%) in those patients of 75 years and older. See Table for details. Discussion We report the impact of age on the management and incidence of critical thromboembolic and bleeding events in patients with AF treated with the direct oral anticoagulant edoxaban. While bleeding rates were low, thromboembolic rates were higher in the elderly. This study complements the PAUSE and DRESDEN studies [ , ], by describing outcomes associated with edoxaban administration, and describing use in a routine clinical practice setting, and provides additional data on the impact of age on outcome. Data was collected, in the first prospective observational multicentre multinational study on the management and outcomes of edoxaban therapy, on 1442 unselected procedures in AF patients. All common comorbidities increased with age, except for obesity and dyslipidaemia, which were lower in patients 85 years and older. Of those patients aged from 75 to 85 years, 21% had a creatinine clearance of ≤ 50 mL/min; 49% of patients 85 years or older had a creatinine clearance of ≤ 50 mL/min. Use of 30 mg edoxaban dose was more common in the older age groups, being taken by 9% of patients < 65 years, and 68% of patients at least 85 years of age. HAS-BLED and CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc scores also increased with age (although of note age is a component of each score). Overall, and as expected [ , ], in older patients the ischemic cardiovascular risk was more clinically significant than the bleeding risk. Despite detailed analysis (Table ) across multiple age cohort groups, no other factors linked to age were identified. This data supports the case that, if dose is appropriately adjusted based upon label requirements, elderly patients do not require modification of management. Edoxaban interruption rates and duration of interruption increased with age. The difference in post-procedural interruption across age groups (> 2-day post-procedural interruption 12.2% in patients < 65 vs. 27.8% in patients ≥ 85 years), suggests physicians tend to be cautious in resuming edoxaban in older patients. Any bleeding complications were rare across all ages. Major bleeding (0.4%), and CRNMB had a combined incidence of 1.0%, with the highest incidence in patients aged 65–74 years (1.6%). There was no discernible relationship between age and bleeding complications. Ischemic or thromboembolic complications were, however, more common in the elderly. Patients aged 65 years and above had combined rates of MB and CRNMB only slightly higher than those < 65 years (1.1% vs. 0.7%) but more ischemic/thromboembolic events (0.8% vs. 0%). Possible explanations include procedures with a higher EHRA bleeding risk being performed in the advanced age groups; or differences in the interruption of edoxaban; or age as an independent risk factor per se. Patients aged 65 years and above had combined rates of MB and CRNMB only slightly higher than those < 65 years (1.1% vs. 0.7%) but more ischemic/thromboembolic events (0.8% vs. 0%). Possible explanations include procedures with a higher EHRA bleeding risk being performed in the advanced age groups; or differences in the interruption of edoxaban; or age as an independent risk factor per se. EHRA risk category is an unlikely explanation in patients of 65 years and above as this factor is only slightly more prevalent than in younger individuals: indeed EHRA minor risk procedures were more common in the elderly (see Fig. ). A more likely explanation is the duration of peri-procedural interruption of edoxaban therapy, which shows a trend toward increased duration with age and appears to be independent from the EHRA bleeding risk. Longer interruption of edoxaban therapy with the intent to reduce bleeding appears to come at the cost of increased risk of thromboembolic/ischemic events. The increase in thromboembolic rates across the age groups was from zero events under age 65 to nine events in the 65-and-older group, while in the same groups the MB/CRNMB rate differed by only 0.4% (0.7% to 1.1%). Prolonged interruption of therapy in the elderly is not associated with a lower risk of major bleeding, but appears to be associated with a higher thromboembolic risk. Other studies have evaluated peri-procedural risk [ , , ] but have not provided results stratified by age. The PAUSE study [ ], which included 3007 procedures, reported post-procedural rates of MB of 1.35% for apixaban, 0.90% for dabigatran, and 1.85% for rivaroxaban cohorts with arterial thromboembolism occurring in 0.16%, 0.6%, and 0.37%, respectively. RE-LY [ ] reported a thromboembolism rate of 0.35% and a MB rate of 1.62% in patients treated with dabigatran. The DRESDEN Registry [ ] reported peri-procedural MB rates of 1.2% and cardiovascular event rates of 1% in a series of 863 procedures in patients who were mainly treated with rivaroxaban. Although different study designs, the event rates in EMIT and all these studies are similar. The four studies together indicate that oral anticoagulation when managed carefully is associated with a low incidence of major haemorrhagic and/or significant thromboembolic events. Several studies have evaluated DOAC use in the elderly; however, many have not collected peri-procedural data. Halperin et al. [ ], reporting the ROCKET-AF comparison of rivaroxaban with VKA in patients with AF, noted increased thromboembolic (4.61 events/100 patient-years vs. 6.07) and MB rates (2.69 vs. 4.86) in the patients aged < 75 or ≥ 75 years, respectively. The RE-LY study [ ] evaluated patients randomized to dabigatran or warfarin. Thromboembolic rates (per patient-year) increased from 1.32% in subjects < 65 years of age, to 1.95% in those aged 80—84 years. The MB rate was 0.14% in subjects < 65 years of age and 5.01% in those aged 80—84 years. In patients with AF not undergoing procedures, the risk of stroke increases 1.5-fold for each decade [ ]. Limitations of study One limitation of this study is a lack of a comparator arm and its restriction to one DOAC, although this study provides data on peri-procedural management of edoxaban for the first time. The much greater sample size required for a comparator would not have been feasible from a timing or economic perspective [ ]. No attempt was made to evaluate the impact of geographical location or ethnicity. Subtle differences in outcome may exist between the various DOAC and/or be influenced by ethnic or geographic factors, although the pharmacodynamic characteristics of the FXa-inhibitors are rather similar and mainly depend on renal function. To account for the challenges of data collection in a registry, patients were provided with memory aids to support data recall, data elements were reviewed at the patient level, and all critical events were centrally adjudicated. Offsetting any loss in quality because of missing data or lack of mechanisms to support compliance is the ability of an observational study to accurately reflect current clinical practice without external influence. Conclusions Detailed age-based subset analysis of the original EMIT data shows minimal differences in patient risk factors linked to age; however, management differed in the elderly. The overall rates of MB and CRNMB were low, and there were no clear age-related trends in incidence. However, the incidence of ischemic complications in the elderly trended higher than in the younger population. This difference is better explained by a longer duration of interruption (both pre- and post-procedural) in the elderly and very elderly, rather than differences in procedural risk, thus supporting the view that increasing age should not be a barrier to adequate anticoagulation [ ]. documents.title: ASH guideline on management of antiphospholipid syndrome

chunks.content: Introduction Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a systemic autoimmune disorder that is defined by arterial, venous, or microvascular thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity, and nonthrombotic manifestations, such as thrombocytopenia and valvular heart disease. , APS is characterized by persistent positivity for antiphospholipid (aPL) antibodies, including anticardiolipin antibodies, anti–β2-glycoprotein I (aβ2GPI) antibodies, and the lupus anticoagulant (LA). Venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is the most frequent initial clinical manifestation. Arterial thromboembolism (ATE) is less common, and catastrophic APS (CAPS) is rare. , , Both are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Long-term anticoagulation is the cornerstone of therapy for thrombotic APS. Most patients are treated with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), particularly warfarin, because of their established efficacy in preventing recurrent thrombosis. However, VKAs present unique challenges in the perioperative setting given their long half-life (∼40 hours) and slow re-establishment of therapeutic anticoagulation, which can lead to 1 to 2 weeks of subtherapeutic anticoagulation during planned interruptions. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are increasingly prescribed, but randomized trials and meta-analyses show that DOACs are inferior to VKAs in high-risk APS, particularly in triple-positive patients. , , , Perioperative management of anticoagulation in APS is challenging. APS is recognized as a high-risk thrombotic condition, and minimizing perioperative recurrent VTE and ATE during interruption of antithrombotic therapy is a clinical priority. , Bridging anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) can be used to mitigate the perioperative risk for thrombosis; however, data from both randomized controlled trials and observational studies of patients without APS suggest that bridging increases postoperative bleeding without clearly reducing perioperative thromboembolism. , , Additional perioperative challenges in patients with APS include the use of concomitant antiplatelet therapy, higher international normalized ratio (INR) targets in recurrent thrombosis, coexisting immune thrombocytopenia, and the perceived risk for CAPS with periprocedural anticoagulation withdrawal and associated surgical stress, all of which further complicate decision-making. , , , , Despite these complexities, the current guidelines, including those of the American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) and the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology, recognize APS as a high-risk condition that warrants individualized perioperative management. , However, these recommendations are based mainly on expert opinion and extrapolation from non-APS populations. There are limited data that describe the perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy for patients with thrombotic APS. The efficacy and safety of the current perioperative anticoagulation management practices in patients with APS are not known. To address these important knowledge gaps, we conducted a single-center, retrospective cohort study to evaluate the risks for postoperative thromboembolism and bleeding after perioperative interruption of anticoagulation in patients with thrombotic APS who underwent planned surgical procedures. Methods Study population We conducted a single-center, retrospective cohort study of anticoagulated patients with thrombotic APS who underwent periprocedural anticoagulation management for planned surgery between 1 January 2016 and 14 April 2025. Patients were identified using a screening roster of all consecutive patients who underwent perioperative assessment for anticoagulation interruption at The Ottawa Hospital (TOH)’s Thrombosis Clinic and a list of filter functions that limited the screening list to patients with any previous documented APS test results conducted at TOH. Filtered outpatient perioperative visits at the TOH Thrombosis Clinic were screened for eligibility. Patients were included if they were ≥18 years of age, had a diagnosis of thrombotic APS (primary or secondary), and were prescribed anticoagulation with a VKA, DOAC, or LMWH. The diagnosis of APS was made by the managing thrombosis physician and was confirmed during record review based on the revised 2006 Sapporo classification criteria, requiring (1) documentation of arterial, venous, or microvascular thrombotic events, and (2) a clinically relevant aPL profile defined as persistently positive LA, anticardiolipin (aCL immunoglobulin G [IgG]/IgM), or aβ2GPI IgG/IgM antibodies, confirmed on ≥2 occasions at least 12 weeks apart. , Eligibility was determined using the 2006 Revised Sapporo Criteria because of the anticipated difficulties in retrospectively classifying patients using the 2023 American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology criteria. Patients with microvascular thrombotic manifestations were included if the treating clinician documented the event as likely attributable to thrombotic APS pathophysiology. Patients who concurrently received antiplatelet therapy or those with advanced chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min or on dialysis) were also included. A planned procedure was defined as a surgery/procedure that occurred ≥72 hours from the decision that a surgical/procedural intervention was needed. Patients were excluded if (1) they had isolated obstetric APS without vascular thrombosis, (2) they underwent a minor procedure that was deemed safe to perform without interrupting anticoagulation therapy (eg, minimal bleeding risk procedures ), (3) they had inadequate documentation regarding the perioperative anticoagulation management, (4) the planned procedure was cancelled, (5) the procedure was emergent/unplanned (<72 hours from decision to intervene), or (6) the patient was pregnant at the time of perioperative interruption. aPL antibody assays aPL testing

A planned procedure was defined as a surgery/procedure that occurred ≥72 hours from the decision that a surgical/procedural intervention was needed. Patients were excluded if (1) they had isolated obstetric APS without vascular thrombosis, (2) they underwent a minor procedure that was deemed safe to perform without interrupting anticoagulation therapy (eg, minimal bleeding risk procedures ), (3) they had inadequate documentation regarding the perioperative anticoagulation management, (4) the planned procedure was cancelled, (5) the procedure was emergent/unplanned (<72 hours from decision to intervene), or (6) the patient was pregnant at the time of perioperative interruption. aPL antibody assays aPL testing at the Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association was performed using the Bio-Rad enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) platform (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA) before 2018. From 2018 onward, Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association transitioned to the BioFlash chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA) platform (Inova Diagnostics, San Diego, CA). Both systems were used to detect aCL IgG/IgM and aβ2GPI IgG/IgM antibodies. The antibody titers were considered positive for both ELISA and CLIA when the values exceeded a nonparametric 99th percentile threshold that was established using a reference population of healthy individuals in accordance with international consensus criteria for APS classification and testing for aPL with solid-phase assays. , This 99th percentile threshold corresponded to a titer of ≥20 GPL/MPL units for ELISA and ≥20 chemiluminescent units for CLIA. LA screening was performed using a lupus-sensitive activated partial thromboplastin time (LA-sensitive aPTT) assay (PTT-SP; Instrumentation Laboratory, Bedford, MA) and a dilute Russell’s viper venom time assay (LaCHECK; Precision BioLogic, Dartmouth, NS, Canada) using a Siemens CS-2100 analyzer. LA confirmation was performed using a dilute Russell’s viper venom time-based confirmatory assay with excess phospholipid (LaSure; Precision BioLogic, Dartmouth, NS, Canada). Conversion thresholds that were established by the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) Scientific and Standardization Committee on Lupus Anticoagulant/Antiphospholipid Antibodies were used to harmonize the semiquantitative interpretation of titer values across the ELISA and CLIA platforms. The aPL titers were categorized as low, moderate, or high using these thresholds ( ). Perioperative anticoagulation management Perioperative anticoagulation management was carried out according to local practice at the TOH Thrombosis Clinic in accordance with contemporary clinical practice guidelines. , Decisions on periprocedural anticoagulation management were made by the treating physician. Procedural bleed risk classification was determined post hoc as minimal bleed risk, low/moderate bleed risk, or high bleed risk based on physician assessment and consistent with the ISTH procedural bleed risk stratification. VKAs were discontinued 5 days before the planned procedure and resumed on the evening of the procedure (postoperative day 0). VKAs were usually resumed using a postoperative loading dose (typically double the maintenance VKA dose for 2 days) at the discretion of the treating physician. , Preoperative INR testing was routinely performed on the day before surgery, and oral vitamin K was administered to patients with an INR >1.5. The decision to use bridging anticoagulation with LMWH was at the treating physician's discretion; LMWH bridging practices typically aligned with clinical practice guideline recommendations. DOACs were interrupted according to the ACCP clinical practice guideline recommendations and Thrombosis Canada guidance, , which are consistent with the approach used in the PAUSE study. DOACs were typically interrupted 1 day before low/moderate bleed–risk procedures and 2 days before high bleed–risk procedures with no dose given on the day of surgery. DOACs were resumed ∼24 hours after low/moderate bleed–risk procedures and 48 to 72 hours after high bleed–risk procedures. Study outcomes The primary outcomes were the 30-day postoperative risks of (1) ATE, (2) VTE, and (3) major bleeding. ATE included ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), and systemic embolism; VTE included pulmonary embolism and DVT (definitions are provided in ). Major bleeding was defined according to the ISTH surgical major bleeding criteria. Secondary outcomes included the 30-day postoperative risks for clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (CRNMB), microvascular thrombotic events, CAPS, and all-cause mortality. CRNMB was defined according to the ISTH criteria. Microvascular thrombotic events were defined as new or recurrent small-vessel manifestations that were attributable to thrombotic APS pathophysiology (eg, digital ischemia and renal thrombotic microangiopathy), as determined by the treating physician and verified by chart review. CAPS was defined according to international consensus criteria. Outcomes were adjudicated in duplicate (M.P., J.R.S.) and were assessed for 30 days following the date of procedure, up to the study end date of April 14 th , 2025. Statistical analysis Demographic and aPL characteristics were summarized on a per-patient basis, whereas procedural and clinical outcome data were analyzed on a per-interruption basis. For patients who underwent >1 perioperative interruption within 30 days, outcomes were measured leading up to the second procedure, and outcomes were then ascertained for 30 days following the second procedure. If multiple procedures occurred consecutively during the same perioperative interruption, the outcomes were ascertained for 30 days following the last procedure

Statistical analysis Demographic and aPL characteristics were summarized on a per-patient basis, whereas procedural and clinical outcome data were analyzed on a per-interruption basis. For patients who underwent >1 perioperative interruption within 30 days, outcomes were measured leading up to the second procedure, and outcomes were then ascertained for 30 days following the second procedure. If multiple procedures occurred consecutively during the same perioperative interruption, the outcomes were ascertained for 30 days following the last procedure in that interruption period. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and proportions. Continuous variables were summarized as means with standard deviations (SDs) for normally distributed data or medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs) for nonnormally distributed data. Exploratory analyses were performed to evaluate procedural and clinical predictors of perioperative bridging use patterns and postoperative bleeding. Each perioperative interruption was analyzed as a distinct clinical episode, and generalized estimating equations (GEE) with a binomial family, a logit link, a robust sandwich variance estimator, and an independence working correlation structure were used to account for within-patient clustering. Given the limited number of postoperative bleeding events, associations between ISTH procedural bleed risk stratification (minimal/low/moderate vs high), urologic or gynecologic procedures (vs all other procedures), and postoperative bleeding were assessed using separate univariable GEE models. In contrast, associations between triple-positive APS status, previous ATE, and receipt of any therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging among VKA-treated patients were examined using a multivariable GEE model (because of an adequate number of bridging exposures). For paired comparisons of preoperative and postoperative bridging intensity, the analyses were limited to VKA-treated patients who received preoperative bridging, and McNemar’s test was used to evaluate changes in preoperative bridging dosing to postoperative dosing. The results are presented as odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs); statistical significance was defined as P < .05. All analyses were exploratory and not adjusted for multiplicity. The 30-day risks for clinical outcomes were reported as proportions with corresponding 95% CIs, calculated using exact methods (Clopper-Pearson). All statistical analyses were performed using Microsoft Excel (version 2511) and R Statistical Software (R Core Team 2025 v4.5.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Ethical approval for this study was granted by the Ottawa Health Sciences Research Ethics Board. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Results Study population and procedure types A total of 1792 perioperative encounters were screened for eligibility between January 2016 and April 2025 ( ), and of those, 172 patients who underwent 282 perioperative interruptions met the criteria for inclusion in the analysis. The mean ± SD age of the cohort was 59.7 ± 13.9 years ( ), and a majority of patients were female (n = 98; 57.0%). Most patients were anticoagulated with VKAs (n = 146; 84.9%); a small proportion were prescribed a DOAC (n = 25; 14.5%). Most patients had a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 (93.9%), whereas a minority were maintained at a higher therapeutic range of 2.5 to 3.5 (4.9%). The mean ± SD CHA 2 DS 2 -Va score (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA or systemic arterial embolism, vascular disease) in patients with atrial fibrillation was 4.4 ± 1.4. Advanced chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min or dialysis) was present in 5.2% of patients, and 4 (2.3%) were on dialysis. Most procedures were performed on an outpatient basis (n = 245; 86.9%), and 112 (39.8%) interruptions were classified as high bleed–risk procedures ( ). Ultrasound-guided renal biopsies accounted for 11.0% (n = 31) of all perioperative interruptions. Twenty patients (7.1%) had thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 × 10 9 /L) within the 6 months before surgery, and 12 patients (4.3%) had thrombocytopenia at the time of surgery. One patient (0.3%) had documented ISTH-defined major bleeding, and 11 (3.9%) had thromboembolism within the 6 months before surgery. aPL testing More than half of the patients had a history of VTE (n = 118; 68.6%) and/or ATE (n = 87; 50.6%). Few patients had documented previous noncriteria manifestations of APS (n = 43; 25.0%), and 12 (7.0%) had a history of Libman-Sacks endocarditis. aPL positivity and the Miyakis classification profiles are outlined in . Among the 172 patients with thrombotic APS, 96 (55.8%) were classified as Miyakis category I (multiple positivity). A quarter of patients (25%) were triple positive. High-titer aPL was recorded in 29 (16.9%) patients with aCL IgG, in 21 (12.2%) with aCL IgM, in 27 (15.7%) with aβ 2 GPI IgG, and 18 (10.5%) with aβ 2 GPI IgM. A total of 53 patients (30.8%) had a concurrent autoimmune disease, including 39 with a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (22.7%). High-titer aPL was recorded in 29 (16.9%) patients with aCL IgG, in 21 (12.2%) with aCL IgM, in 27 (15.7%) with aβ 2 GPI IgG, and 18 (10.5%) with aβ 2 GPI IgM. A total of 53 patients (30.8%) had a concurrent autoimmune disease, including 39 with a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (22.7%). Perioperative anticoagulation management VKAs were discontinued for 5 days preoperatively (last dose on postoperative day [POD] ˗6) in nearly all interruptions (95.4%; ). VKAs were resumed in the evening on the day of surgery in most patients (median, POD 0; IQR, POD 0-1). Most (81.2%) restarted on POD 0, and 16.1% resumed on POD 1. A total of 21 patients (7.4%) had a preoperative INR of ≥1.5, and preoperative vitamin K was required in 3.2% of interruptions because of INR ≥1.5 on POD ˗1. Warfarin was resumed using a postoperative loading dose in 102 (43.2%) interruptions. For DOAC-treated patients ( ), the median duration of preoperative interruption was 72 hours (IQR, 60-72) for high bleed–risk procedures and 48 hours (IQR, 42-66) for minimal/low/moderate bleed–risk procedures. Postoperative DOAC resumption occurred at a median of 60 hours (IQR, 36-72) after high bleed–risk procedures and 36 hours (IQR, 36-36) after minimal/low/moderate bleed–risk procedures. Concurrent antiplatelet therapy was documented in 12.7% of interruptions; antiplatelet agents were continued in more than half of the interruptions that involved antiplatelet-treated patients (58.3%). Bridging practices among VKA-treated patients are summarized in . In terms of preoperative bridging, 90 interruptions (42.9%) involved any therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging, whereas 77 (36.7%) involved prophylactic-dose bridging and 43 (20.5%) involved no bridging. Among VKA-treated patients who received any preoperative bridging (n = 188), 35.1% received therapeutic-dose bridging preoperatively and were transitioned to prophylactic-dose postoperatively (i.e., de-escalation). Otherwise, 43.6% maintained prophylactic dosing from before to after the procedure. Only 0.5% escalated from prophylactic preoperative bridging to therapeutic intensity postoperatively, and 20.7% remained on therapeutic bridging throughout. A pairwise analysis demonstrated significantly higher odds of de-escalating bridging postoperatively (McNemar paired OR, 66.0; 95% CI, 9.1-500.0; P < .0001), reflecting substantially more transitions from preoperative therapeutic-dose bridging to postoperative prophylactic bridging (or no bridging) than the reverse. Triple-positive patients were more likely to have received any therapeutic-dose bridging therapy than those who did not have triple positivity (72.2% vs 30.0%; OR, 7.6; 95% CI, 3.2-18.2; P < .001). Similarly, therapeutic bridging was more commonly administered for patients with a history of ATE than for those without a previous ATE (53.1% vs 27.4%; OR, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.5-7.8; P = .003). Clinical outcomes There were 2 postoperative ATEs, yielding a 30-day postoperative ATE risk of 0.7% (95% CI, 0.2-2.6). The first event was a TIA on POD 13 after an umbilical hernia repair (54-year-old male on warfarin, INR target of 2.0 to 3.0, no concurrent ASA, aCL positive, history of recurrent stroke/TIA) that occurred despite resuming warfarin using a loading dose and receiving postoperative LMWH prophylaxis (dalteparin 5000 IU subcutaneous [SQ] once daily until INR > 2.0; INR was 3.4 at presentation with TIA). The second event was a systemic embolism (right superficial femoral artery) on POD 2 after a facet injection (59-year-old male on warfarin, INR target of 2.0 to 3.0, taking 325 mg ASA daily, aCL positive, history of TIA) requiring catheter-directed thrombolysis on POD 5. This occurred despite resuming warfarin with a loading dose, receiving postoperative LMWH prophylaxis (dalteparin 5000 IU SQ once daily until INR > 2.0), and aspirin 325 mg daily starting on POD 1. There was 1 central line–associated upper extremity DVT (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0) that occurred on POD 10. There were 2 major bleeding events during the 30-day follow-up period, yielding a 30-day major bleeding risk of 0.7% (95% CI, 0.2-2.6; ). Both occurred in patients who underwent high bleed–risk procedures. The first event occurred following a kidney biopsy in a patient on warfarin (preoperative INR = 1.1, no concurrent antiplatelet therapy), which led to a perinephric hematoma with interval expansion on repeat ultrasound and an associated drop in hemoglobin of >20 g/L. The second event was fatal and occurred in a 46-year-old female (aCL positive, previous recurrent VTE, thrombocytopenia) following a right hemipelvectomy (high bleed–risk procedure; estimated blood loss 3.5 L) owing to nonmetastatic myxofibrosarcoma. The patient (warfarin at baseline, bridging with prophylactic fondaparinux owing to a history of injection reaction to LMWH) developed iliac artery rupture with massive bleeding on POD 8, requiring activation of a massive transfusion protocol and leading to immediate pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest. Despite urgent vessel ligation, right lower-limb amputation, and massive transfusion, the patient developed multiorgan failure and died

The patient (warfarin at baseline, bridging with prophylactic fondaparinux owing to a history of injection reaction to LMWH) developed iliac artery rupture with massive bleeding on POD 8, requiring activation of a massive transfusion protocol and leading to immediate pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest. There were 9 CRNMB events ( ), corresponding to a 30-day risk of 3.2% (95% CI, 1.7-6.0). Eight events occurred in patients who were anticoagulated with warfarin, and 1 occurred in a patient who was treated with rivaroxaban. High bleed–risk surgery (vs minimal/low/moderate) was associated with significantly greater odds of postoperative bleeding (composite of major bleeding + CRNMB: OR, 7.3; 95% CI, 1.5-35.4; P = .01). Similarly, undergoing a urologic or gynecologic procedure (vs all others) was also associated with substantially increased odds of postoperative bleeding (OR, 6.6; 95% CI, 1.8-24.5; P = .005). Postoperative microvascular APS occurred in 2 patients (0.7%; 95% CI, 0.2-2.6). The first occurred on POD 10 in a triple-positive patient who developed biopsy-proven thrombotic microangiopathy of a transplanted kidney, which led to graft rejection. The second happened on POD 8 in another triple-positive patient and presented as an adrenal gland hemorrhage. Clinicians attributed this event to microvascular thrombosis and adrenal infarction, which subsequently led to adrenal insufficiency. This occurred in a 25-year-old triple-positive APS patient with ulcerative colitis who underwent a colonoscopy. On POD 8, the patient developed acalculous cholecystitis, adrenal hemorrhage, and thrombocytopenia while receiving prophylactic tinzaparin at a dose of 4500 IU SQ daily. A heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) ELISA was positive (optical density OD, 1.6), but functional testing (serotonin release assay) was negative, confirming the absence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. This single event met the criteria for probable CAPS (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0), corresponding to a 30-day risk of 1.4% (95% CI, 0.0-7.6) among triple-positive patients. There was 1 death during the 30-day follow-up (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0) that was attributed to fatal bleeding (outlined earlier). Discussion Data to guide the perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy for patients with thrombotic APS are limited. Herein, we report results from a single-center, retrospective cohort of anticoagulated adults with thrombotic APS who underwent a planned invasive procedure or surgery. Perioperative anticoagulation management was generally consistent with contemporary guideline-directed practice. The 30-day risks for ATE, VTE, and ISTH-defined major bleeding were low and comparable with contemporary non-APS cohorts. CAPS, a recognized concern in the setting of anticoagulation withdrawal and surgical stress, was rare. Our findings suggest that contemporary perioperative anticoagulation strategies, when applied with individualized attention to thrombotic and bleeding risk, can be safely implemented in patients with APS. Perioperative management in our cohort followed a consistent framework that reflected both guideline-concordant practices and local practice patterns. Most VKA-treated patients received some form of parenteral bridging anticoagulation, reflecting the ACCP guideline designation of APS as a high thrombotic–risk condition for which bridging may be appropriate. Concurrent antiplatelet therapy was uncommon (∼13%), and complicating perioperative thrombocytopenia was rare (4.3%). Few patients had a higher INR target (2.5-3.5; ∼5%). Holding warfarin for 5 days before surgery led to INR normalization (INR < 1.5) in most (∼92.6%) VKA-treated patients. In a previous single-center APS surgical cohort, guideline-concordant periprocedural anticoagulation management was associated with fewer thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications (7% vs 33%; OR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.02-0.81; P = .04), and an INR of ≤1.5 at surgery was associated with fewer major bleeding events (6% vs 29%; OR, 0.19; 95% CI, 0.02-0.98; P = .05). The 30-day risks for major bleeding (0.7%; 95% CI, 0.2-2.6) and CRNMB (3.2%; 95% CI, 1.7-6.0) compared favorably with those of contemporary non-APS cohorts. The 30-day risks for major bleeding in the BRIDGE trial were 1.3% and 3.2% in the nonbridging and bridging arms, respectively, whereas the risks ranged from 0.9% to 1.9% in the PAUSE study depending on the DOAC in question. , Importantly, in our study, major bleeding events were attributed to anatomic and procedural factors rather than anticoagulation status at bleeding onset. Most bleeding events occurred after a high bleed–risk procedure, including both of the recorded major bleeding events, and more than half of the bleeding events involved urologic or gynecologic procedures (renal biopsy, hysterectomy, transurethral resection of bladder tumor, uterine ablation). Few early bleeding events occurred during therapeutic-dose bridging; most occurred after appropriate perioperative interruption with INR values within the expected range at surgery. Taken together, these findings underscore the importance of carefully considering the type of procedure (eg, urologic procedures) and postoperative bleeding risk when devising a perioperative anticoagulation management plan. Data from non-APS populations indicate that bridging increases postoperative bleeding without clearly reducing the thromboembolism risk, but these studies enrolled patients with lower-risk indications (eg, atrial fibrillation) and may not be generalizable to APS. , APS is both clinically and biologically heterogeneous. More than half of our cohort met Miyakis category I criteria, one-quarter were triple-positive, and moderate to high aPL titers were observed across multiple isotypes. These features typically indicate a higher thrombotic risk. Our cohort also demonstrated a substantial burden of clinical thrombotic risk factors. More than half had a previous ATE, the majority had a history of VTE, and nearly one-third had a concurrent autoimmune disease. Clinicians seemed to incorporate APS-related thrombotic risk into their perioperative decision-making. Patients with triple-positive APS and those with a previous ATE were more likely to receive therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging. Our findings suggest that a one-size-fits-all approach is unlikely to be appropriate in APS. Tailoring perioperative anticoagulation management to both APS-related thrombotic risk and procedural bleed risk seems to have been both feasible and safe in this heterogeneous, higher-risk cohort. Postoperative bridging in our cohort frequently comprised prophylactic-dose LMWH after high bleed–risk procedures; this may, in part, represent local extrapolation of postoperative dose modulation concepts that have been evaluated in other high thrombotic–risk populations (eg, patients with a mechanical heart valve), recognizing that therapeutic-dose anticoagulation in the immediate postoperative period is a shared driver of major bleeding risk. Given the observational design and low event counts, this practice pattern should be interpreted cautiously. Both ATE events occurred while patients were receiving postoperative LMWH prophylaxis. Microvascular events were uncommon overall (0.7%) but occurred exclusively in triple-positive patients; 1 event met the criteria for probable CAPS, which happened while the patient was receiving postoperative prophylactic LMWH. Although definitive causal inferences cannot be made, these observations, together with published case reports describing rapid, severe thrombotic events in triple-positive secondary APS (often with concomitant systemic autoimmune disease) after brief warfarin interruption despite LMWH bridging, supports considering therapeutic-dose bridging and tightly timed periprocedural anticoagulation strategies that minimize time off anticoagulation in the highest-risk phenotypes (ie, triple-positive APS and/or previous ATE). Conversely, for lower-risk phenotypes and/or higher bleed–risk procedures, initiating prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation early in the postoperative period with escalation as surgical hemostasis permits may offer a pragmatic balance. Prospective studies are needed to confirm optimal strategies across APS phenotypes. This study has several strengths. To our knowledge, it represents the largest, single-center cohort that evaluated perioperative anticoagulation management in patients with thrombotic APS. Perioperative antithrombotic strategies at our center followed relatively standardized workflows, enabling detailed characterization of warfarin interruption intervals, preoperative INR assessment, vitamin K use, LMWH bridging dose and timing, and postoperative VKA resumption practices. The outcome definitions adhered to widely recognized international standards, and the cohort encompassed a broad mix of invasive procedures with more than one-third classified as high bleed–risk procedures. TOH is the regional referral center for thrombosis, APS, and stroke, and patients with APS undergo close, frequent monitoring, including regular pharmacist-specialist contacts for VKA management. Consequently, although retrospective analyses are inherently susceptible to variable documentation and information bias, the likelihood of missing major thrombotic or bleeding outcomes is low. Important limitations should also be acknowledged. First, the measurement of aPL antibodies is itself a known challenge; our cohort spanned a period during which laboratory methodology transitioned from ELISA to CLIA platforms. Although we harmonized titers using published ISTH conversion thresholds and applied a 99th percentile positivity cutoff, some misclassification remains possible. Second, several patients underwent multiple perioperative interruptions, which led to more interruptions than there were patients. Although GEE models were used to account for within-patient clustering when evaluating bridging patterns and overall bleeding risk, events were too few to support multivariable modelling of clinical outcomes. Thus, the determined estimates and their CIs should be interpreted cautiously. Third, serial postoperative INR trajectories were not uniformly available across interruption episodes, precluding estimation of time spent below therapeutic range and time to reattain a therapeutic INR after warfarin resumption.

Fourth, concomitant hydroxychloroquine use was not systematically captured, limiting assessment of its potential influence on perioperative thrombotic and bleeding outcomes. Finally, as a retrospective, single-center analysis, perioperative decisions, including bridging intensity, were not protocolized and event counts were low, leading to wide confidence intervals for the event estimates. In summary, patients with thrombotic APS who underwent planned interruption of anticoagulation at our center experienced low 30-day risks for ATE, VTE, and major bleeding when managed using contemporary perioperative strategies. Clinical practice patterns reflected a risk-adapted approach. Clinicians used therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging more often in patients with triple-positive APS or a history of ATE. They used prophylactic-dose bridging more frequently after high bleed–risk procedures. Individualized management that integrates APS-related thrombotic risk, procedural bleed risk, and clinical context seems safe. The occurrence of microvascular APS manifestations, including 1 case of probable CAPS, underscores that high-risk phenotypes remain vulnerable during anticoagulation withdrawal and merit heightened vigilance. Future research should focus on multicenter prospective studies to refine risk stratification, define optimal bridging strategies across APS phenotypes, and better characterize clinical outcomes in the perioperative setting.
